quick_hits: Eleven Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks wintered near Sarasota in 1981–82. Several stayed through summer, the flock grew, and the species eventually spread across nearly all of Florida. The founding flock is thought to have reached Sarasota on its own, possibly across the Gulf from the Yucatán.
Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks regularly perch in trees, on fence rails, and even on utility lines. Their long legs and upright stance are part of why they can look more goose-like than most ducks.
They usually nest in tree cavities. Within a day or two of hatching, the ducklings climb to the entrance and drop to the ground, then follow their parents to feeding areas.
Unlike most ducks, both parents take turns incubating the eggs and both care for the ducklings.
species.range_and_origin: Native from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America into South America. Its North American range has expanded dramatically northward and eastward in recent decades, and the species is now established across most of Florida.
more_information: Tree cavities are the usual nest site, but these ducks readily use nest boxes and will sometimes nest on the ground. They build very little inside a cavity — the eggs may simply rest on whatever debris has collected there.
Females sometimes lay eggs in one another's nests. When several contribute to the same cavity, a nest can hold fifty or more eggs, far beyond what one pair could produce or successfully incubate.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A tall, long-legged duck with a long neck and unusually upright stance. On land it can look more goose-like than most ducks.

blocks.label: Markings
blocks.text: A bright pink bill and long pink legs, a chestnut breast and back, a black belly, and a pale gray face with a neat white eye-ring. A bold white stripe crosses the wing. Males and females look alike.

blocks.label: Juveniles
blocks.text: Duller and browner, with a gray bill and pale legs, and without the sharp black belly. The white wing stripe is still there and still useful.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: In flight, the neck stretches forward and the long legs trail behind the tail. A broad white wing patch becomes conspicuous.

identification.what_to_look_for: Start with the pink bill and long pink legs. In flight, look for the broad white wing patch and the legs extending beyond the tail. A flock's whistling often gives the birds away before you see them.

species.diet: Mostly seeds, grasses, aquatic plants and grains. They feed on land and in shallow water, dabbling at the surface or tipping forward to reach submerged plants. Insects, snails and other small animals are a much smaller part of it. Much of the feeding happens at night.
species.behavior: Highly social, often gathering in noisy flocks. They spend much of the day resting near water and do much of their feeding after dark. On land they walk easily on unusually long legs.
species.sounds: Listen for a clear, high whistle, especially from birds in flight. A moving flock can produce a chorus loud enough to reveal the birds before you see them.
species.ecological_role: Eggs and ducklings are prey for snakes, raccoons and other wetland predators. Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks also use the same limited tree cavities sought by Wood Ducks, and both species readily use nest boxes.
species.habitat: Shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, and wetlands bordered by trees — particularly areas with standing or dead trees suitable for cavity nesting. Also highly comfortable in human-modified landscapes: urban retention ponds, golf courses, suburban parks, agricultural fields, and flooded pastures. FWC notes they can adapt to almost any habitat in rural and urban areas as long as water and nearby tree cover are available.
species.where_to_look: Look around shallow ponds and wet grassy edges, especially where trees stand close to the water. This species readily uses retention ponds, parks, golf courses, flooded fields and other developed landscapes. Flocks often rest near water during the day or perch in nearby trees.
species.when_to_see: Look year-round. Through the day they often rest near water; early morning and late afternoon bring more local movement. Much of their feeding happens after dark.

size.length: about 20 inches long, with a wingspan close to three feet

interaction.guidance: Watch from a comfortable distance and let the birds decide how close to come. Do not feed them; natural food is plentiful, and feeding wildlife changes normal behavior.

invasive.notes: This is not an introduced exotic. Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks expanded into Florida under their own power and are now established residents.

conservation.status: Widespread and increasing in North America, with the breeding range still expanding. Not considered threatened; listed as Least Concern by the IUCN.

seasonality.note: Breeding occurs in Florida, so pairs and family groups with ducklings may be seen during the warmer part of the year.

species.teaser: A tree-perching duck that whistles instead of quacking — and expanded into Florida without being introduced by people.

how_it_lives.text: Highly social, often gathering in noisy flocks. They spend much of the day resting near water and do much of their feeding after dark.
On land they walk easily on those long legs rather than waddling. In the air the flight is slow and shallow-winged, with the feet trailing well behind the tail.

what_it_does_here.text: Eggs and ducklings are prey for snakes, raccoons and other wetland predators. Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks also use the same limited tree cavities sought by Wood Ducks, and both species readily use nest boxes.
Trees provide both nest sites and daytime perches. The ducks usually nest in natural cavities, while grasses, sedges and aquatic plants around wetlands provide much of their food.

what_it_does_here.label: Too many eggs for one mother
what_it_does_here.text: Females sometimes lay in one another's nests. When several contribute to the same cavity, it can hold fifty or more eggs — far beyond what a single pair could produce, let alone incubate.

species.plant_connections: Trees provide both nest sites and daytime perches. The ducks usually nest in natural cavities, while grasses, sedges and aquatic plants around wetlands provide much of their food.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Browner overall, and without the bold white wing patch. Young Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks lack the pink bill of adults, so the wing pattern is the more reliable difference.

quick_hits: A forager that finds a good patch of flowers can tell other workers where it is. Inside the hive, she performs a waggle dance whose direction points toward the food relative to the sun, while the length of the waggle run conveys distance.

A worker's jobs change as she ages. Young workers clean cells, feed larvae and build comb inside the colony. Older workers become guards and foragers, spending the last part of their lives outside collecting nectar and pollen.
Honey bees are not native to the Americas. European colonists brought them to North America in the 1600s, and managed and free-living colonies are now widespread.
A colony reproduces by swarming. The old queen leaves with a large part of the workers, and they cluster nearby — often as a hanging mass on a branch — while scouts search for a cavity to move into.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, where many subspecies evolved across a wide range of climates. No subspecies is native to the Americas. Colonists brought the bee to North America beginning in the early 1600s, and managed and free-living colonies are now established across the continent.
more_information: Queens make sounds. A newly emerged queen produces a high-pitched tooting, answered by muffled quacking from queens still sealed in their cells — part of how a colony settles which queen will lead it after a swarm.

A colony behaves like a larger organism. Tens of thousands of workers regulate temperature, rear young, store food, defend the nest and exchange information without a central individual directing every action.

blocks.label: Pollen baskets
blocks.text: Look at the hind legs of a foraging worker. Honey bees pack collected pollen into flattened baskets there, sometimes forming conspicuous yellow, orange or cream-colored loads.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Workers are about half an inch long — roughly the size of a watermelon seed. The bee on a flower will almost always be a worker.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Usually brown to orange-brown, with dark and paler bands across the abdomen and dense hairs on the thorax. Color varies considerably among honey bees.

blocks.label: Similar insects
blocks.text: Bumble bees are generally larger and much furrier. Paper wasps have a narrow waist, less body hair and longer-looking legs. Pollen packed onto the hind legs is a strong clue that you are looking at a bee.

identification.what_to_look_for: Start with the hind legs. A worker carrying a packed yellow or orange pollen load is easy to recognize.

species.diet: Nectar supplies carbohydrates and is stored as honey. Pollen supplies protein and other nutrients, especially for developing young. Workers also carry water back to the colony.
species.behavior: Workers communicate largely through scent, and a forager can also perform dances on the comb that direct nestmates toward profitable food.
species.ecological_role: Honey bees pollinate many crops and garden plants. In North America they are introduced pollinators, and dense managed or free-living colonies can compete with native bees for flowers. The size of that effect varies among habitats and bee communities.
species.habitat: Highly adaptable; colonies nest in enclosed cavities — hollow trees, rock crevices, wall voids, and empty structures — wherever a cavity of roughly 10 to 40 liters can be found. Foragers exploit any landscape with flowering plants within roughly a 2-mile radius of the nest: gardens, parks, forest edges, wetland margins, and agricultural fields all fall within their foraging range.
species.where_to_look: Look wherever many flowers are open at once. Flowering shrubs, trees and garden beds can draw workers throughout the day; pollen packed onto the hind legs is often visible without getting very close.
species.when_to_see: Honey bees forage year-round in southwest Florida whenever flowers and weather permit. Warm, dry days with many plants in bloom offer the best chance of seeing them.

size.length: Workers are about half an inch long. Queens are somewhat longer; males are stockier and have much larger eyes.

danger.people: A honey-bee worker can sting if trapped or if its colony is threatened. A sting usually causes temporary pain and swelling, but severe allergic reactions can occur. If a stinger remains in the skin, remove it promptly. Trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, faintness, or other signs of a severe allergic reaction require emergency medical care.
danger.pets: Dogs and cats that snap at bees can be stung, usually on the muzzle or in the mouth. A single sting is normally minor, but stings inside the mouth or throat, or many at once, need a veterinarian. Keep pets away from hives and swarms.

interaction.guidance: Foraging bees on flowers are usually focused on collecting food. Watch without swatting or handling them. Do not approach or disturb a colony or large cluster of bees; alert park staff instead.

invasive.notes: Western Honey Bees are introduced in Florida, not native. They are not generally managed as an invasive pest, but high densities of honey bees can compete with native bees for floral resources and may contribute to pathogen transmission.

conservation.status: Western Honey Bees are abundant and widely managed in Florida and are not a local conservation concern. Managed colonies nevertheless face serious health problems from parasites, pathogens, pesticides and other stresses.

seasonality.note: Foraging follows flowering and temperature rather than the calendar. Activity slows on the coldest days but does not stop.

species.teaser: A forager can return to the colony and tell other workers the direction and distance to a good patch of flowers.

how_it_lives.text: Workers communicate largely through scent. A forager can also perform dances on the comb that direct nestmates toward profitable food.
Nectar supplies carbohydrates and is stored as honey. Pollen supplies protein and other nutrients, especially for developing young. Workers also bring water back to the colony.

species.plant_connections: Flowers supply nectar and pollen, but honey bees collect other plant materials too. Workers gather sticky resins from buds and bark and turn them into propolis, which helps seal and line the nest. Different plants become important as flowering changes through the year.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The paper wasp has a narrow waist, a nearly hairless body, and folds its wings lengthwise at rest. A honey bee is furry, thick-waisted, and often carrying pollen on its hind legs.

quick_hits: Some antlion larvae build funnel-shaped traps in loose sand. The walls are steep enough to collapse under struggling prey, and the buried larva can flick sand upward to knock an escaping insect back toward its jaws.
A Bright Futures student first showed us these animals at Palma Sola. He noticed the small pits in the sand, explained what made them, and uncovered a larva for us to photograph.
Florida has 22 antlion species in nine genera, giving the state the richest antlion fauna in the eastern United States.
species.range_and_origin: Antlions occur on every continent except Antarctica and are most abundant in warm, dry, sandy regions. All Florida species are native, and sandy peninsular Florida — including Manatee County — sits well within their range year-round.
more_information: Owlflies were traditionally placed in their own family. Genetic studies now place them within the antlion family, which is why both groups may appear together in modern classifications.

blocks.label: Look for the pit
blocks.text: The easiest sign is a small funnel-shaped pit in dry, loose sand. The larva waits buried at the bottom, usually with only its curved jaws near the surface.

blocks.label: If you see the larva
blocks.text: The larva is squat and gray-brown, with a broad head and a pair of long, curved jaws. Many are around half an inch long.

blocks.label: Adult antlion
blocks.text: Adults look somewhat like drab damselflies, with long net-veined wings and clubbed antennae. They often come to lights at night.

blocks.label: Owlfly
blocks.text: Owlflies belong to the same family but hunt flying insects at dusk. They look dragonfly-like, with a wingspan to about four inches and antennae nearly as long as the body — no Florida dragonfly has antennae anything like that.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for the pits rather than the animal. Small cones in dry sand under an overhang or at the base of a tree each mark one larva waiting below.

species.diet: Larvae are sit-and-wait predators of ants and other small ground-dwelling invertebrates. They pierce prey with hollow jaws, inject fluids that liquefy the tissues, and drink the contents. Adult antlions take nectar and pollen and some small insects; owlflies hunt moths and gnats in flight.
species.behavior: The larva waits buried at the bottom of its pit and moves only backward. Adult antlions are weak, mostly nocturnal fliers drawn to lights; owlflies hunt on the wing at dusk and dawn and perch by day with the abdomen cocked up like a broken twig.
species.ecological_role: Antlion larvae prey on ants and other small invertebrates in sandy habitats. They in turn are eaten or parasitized by other animals. Adult owlflies hunt flying insects.
species.habitat: Antlion larvae require dry, fine, loose sand that stays protected from direct rain — the undersides of building overhangs, the bases of trees, open sandy clearings, and sandy path margins are all classic sites. Adult antlions and owlflies use open woodland edges, dry scrub, meadows, and any habitat with flying insects and access to suitable oviposition sites. Palma Sola Botanical Park's sandy soils and sheltered dry spots under large trees and structures are well-suited to supporting larvae.
species.where_to_look: Look for small funnel-shaped pits in dry, loose sand protected from rain — under overhangs, beneath trees, beside structures and along sheltered sandy path edges. Adult antlions may come to lights after dark.
species.when_to_see: Larval pits can be found year-round where dry sand stays protected from rain. Adults are most likely on warm nights.

size.length: Larvae are often around half an inch long. Adults are much larger, with long wings and slender bodies.

danger.people: They pose no meaningful danger to people. A larva may pinch if handled, but adults do not sting.

interaction.guidance: Watch a pit without disturbing it. The larva may be visible only as the tips of its jaws at the bottom. Avoid collapsing the sides; rebuilding costs the animal time and energy.

invasive.notes: All Florida antlion and owlfly species are native. Not listed as invasive by any Florida authority.

conservation.status: No Florida or federal conservation concern. Florida's 22 native antlion species are common and widespread, and the state holds the richest antlion fauna in the eastern United States. No species in this family is listed as threatened or endangered in Florida.

seasonality.note: Pits persist wherever sheltered dry sand does. Heavy rain erodes them, and they are rebuilt afterward.

species.teaser: The larva digs a pit by moving backward through loose sand, then waits buried at the bottom. When prey tries to climb out, it flicks sand upward and sends the slope sliding.

how_it_lives.text: The larva waits buried at the bottom of the pit. When a small insect slides within reach, the antlion grips it with hollow jaws, injects digestive fluids, and draws the liquefied tissues back through the jaws.

how_it_lives.label: Two different adults
how_it_lives.text: Adult antlions are weak, erratic fliers that come to lights at night and spend the day motionless on a dry stem or strip of bark. Owlflies hunt on the wing at dusk and dawn much as dragonflies do, then perch by day with the abdomen cocked up, doing a convincing impression of a broken twig.

species.plant_connections: Plants help create the sheltered ground these larvae need. Dry sand beneath broad tree canopies, exposed roots, overhangs and other rain-protected spots can remain suitable for pits when surrounding ground is wet.

quick_hits: The Giant Swallowtail is among Florida's largest butterflies, with broad dark wings crossed by yellow bands. Its long glides make it conspicuous over gardens and woodland edges.
The caterpillar is called an orangedog because it feeds on citrus and other plants in the rue family. Its mottled brown, white and gray pattern resembles a bird dropping.
If disturbed, the caterpillar can extend a forked orange organ called an osmeterium from behind its head. It releases a strong odor that helps deter predators.
In south Florida, adults can be seen throughout the year. Farther north, the flight season is more restricted.
species.range_and_origin: The Eastern Giant Swallowtail is native to eastern North America, ranging from southern New England and the Great Lakes south through Florida, the Caribbean, and into Mexico. It is common throughout the entire state of Florida and is one of the most frequently seen large butterflies in the region. Florida and the deep South are the only parts of the eastern United States where the species can overwinter and remain active year-round. Populations once thought to extend west to South America are now recognized as a separate species, the Western Giant Swallowtail (Papilio rumiko), based on DNA evidence; the butterfly at Palma Sola is the eastern form.
more_information: The round eggs are orange-colored and laid singly on host leaves.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: A very large swallowtail, usually around four to six inches across. Females often run slightly larger than males.

blocks.label: Upperside
blocks.text: Wings are dark brown to black with two bold diagonal bands of yellow spots — one crossing the forewings, one sweeping across the hindwings — that meet near the body to form a rough X-shape. Hindwings have yellow-centered tails and a small blue-and-red spot near the inner margin.

blocks.label: Underside
blocks.text: Largely yellow with black borders and blue scaling near the body — a striking contrast to the dark upperside. A small red patch on the ventral hindwing helps distinguish this species from the similar but much rarer Schaus' Swallowtail.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: Broad wings held flat, with long slow beats interspersed with extended glides.

blocks.label: Caterpillar
blocks.text: Brown, gray, and white with a creamy saddle mark — a convincing bird-dropping mimic at every stage. Mature larvae may also show faint eyespot-like markings. When disturbed, the orange-red forked osmeterium everts from just behind the head.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a very large dark swallowtail crossed by broad yellow bands. It often alternates slow wingbeats with long glides. The caterpillar rests in the open and looks like a bird dropping.

species.diet: Caterpillars eat the leaves of plants in the citrus and rue family. Adults drink nectar from a wide range of flowers.
species.behavior: Adults glide more than they flap, and males run patrol routes along wooded edges looking for females. Females lay eggs singly on the upper surface of a host leaf. Caterpillars feed at night and rest exposed by day.
species.ecological_role: Caterpillars consume leaves of citrus-family plants and are prey for birds, spiders and predatory insects, as well as parasitoid wasps and flies. Adults visit many kinds of flowers and can carry pollen between them.
species.habitat: Forest margins, citrus groves, suburban gardens, parks, and open woodland edges — essentially any landscape that supports plants in the Rutaceae family. In central and south Florida the species is equally at home in native scrub and hammock edges as in ornamental plantings.
species.where_to_look: Watch flowering beds and sunny woodland edges for adults. For caterpillars, check plants in the citrus family, especially citrus, wild lime and Hercules' club. The mottled larvae often rest openly on leaves or stems.
species.when_to_see: Adults can be seen through much of the year in southwest Florida, especially on warm sunny days.

size.length: Wingspan usually about four to six inches.
size.lifespan: Adults live roughly two to four weeks.

danger.people: Completely harmless to people. No sting, no meaningful bite, no toxins. The caterpillar's osmeterium secretion is a mild chemical deterrent aimed at small invertebrates and is not a hazard to humans.

interaction.guidance: Watch without touching. Handling can damage a butterfly's wings and scales. Leave caterpillars on their host plants.

invasive.notes: A native species with deep roots in Florida's ecosystems. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Least Concern (IUCN). Ranked G5 (globally secure) by NatureServe. Common and widespread throughout eastern North America; not listed as threatened at the federal or Florida state level. No special conservation protections required.

seasonality.note: Multiple broods overlap, so adults and caterpillars may both be present. Cooler days reduce activity.

species.teaser: The caterpillar resembles a bird dropping and feeds on citrus and its wild relatives. Citrus growers have long called it the orangedog.

how_it_lives.text: A strong flier that spends most of its time gliding — with that wingspan it can cover ground without much flapping. Males run patrol routes through wooded edges and citrus groves looking for females, mostly in the afternoon.

how_it_lives.label: A caterpillar dressed as bird droppings
how_it_lives.text: Females lay eggs singly on the upper surface of a leaf. The caterpillar often rests exposed on a leaf or stem during the day, where its mottled pattern resembles a bird dropping, and feeds at night.
Multiple broods follow one another through the year in Florida, so adults and caterpillars can be present at the same time.

species.plant_connections: The caterpillar can eat only a limited group of host plants, chiefly members of the citrus family. In Florida these include native wild lime and Hercules' club as well as cultivated citrus. Adults use a much wider range of flowering plants for nectar.

quick_hits: Evening bats emerge soon after sunset, sometimes while there is still enough light to follow them with the eye. They often forage over water and along woodland edges with a relatively slow, steady flight.
Females usually have twins. Together, newborn pups can weigh about half as much as their mother does after giving birth — an unusually large reproductive investment for a mammal.
Evening bats do not use caves. They roost in tree cavities, behind loose bark and sometimes in buildings or other structures.
Newborn pups are blind and nearly hairless, but they develop quickly and can fly at about three weeks old.
species.range_and_origin: The evening bat ranges across the eastern and midwestern United States from the Great Lakes south through Florida and into Veracruz, Mexico. It is a native species throughout its North American range. In Florida, it is common statewide except for the Keys, and Manatee County sits well within the heart of its Florida distribution. Northern populations migrate south in fall to overwinter in the warmer southern portions of the range; Florida bats typically move far shorter distances and may remain active year-round during mild winters.
more_information: In autumn, evening bats from the northern part of the range build fat reserves and travel south; one banded bat was recovered more than 340 miles from where it was marked. Florida's bats largely skip the journey.

blocks.label: At dusk
blocks.text: A small dark-brown bat with relatively slow, steady flight, often hunting over water or along a woodland edge.

blocks.label: Up close
blocks.text: The fur is dark brown above and paler below, with dark wings and short ears. Evening bats resemble several other Florida bats and usually cannot be identified confidently from a brief view in flight.

identification.what_to_look_for: Watch the flight rather than the markings. A small bat working slowly back and forth over the same stretch of water at dusk is the likeliest thing you will see.

species.diet: They eat flying insects, especially beetles, along with moths, flies, mosquitoes and flying ants.
species.behavior: Nocturnal and colonial. Bats emerge soon after dusk and hunt again before dawn, flying slowly enough to pick insects out of cluttered air along an edge or over water. Females gather in maternity colonies; adult males roost separately.
species.sounds: Its hunting calls are ultrasonic and normally beyond human hearing. A bat detector can convert them into audible sound. Mothers and pups also make social calls inside the roost.
species.ecological_role: Evening bats are nocturnal predators of beetles, moths and other flying insects. Their dependence on tree cavities and loose bark also makes mature trees and standing dead wood important habitat.
species.habitat: A forest bat that favors wooded areas near water — rivers, ponds, wetland margins, and forest clearings where insect prey concentrates. Roost sites are tree cavities, spaces behind loose bark on large snags, Spanish moss clumps, and palm frond bases in Florida; buildings, bridges, bat houses, and utility-pole brackets are used where natural sites are limited. Never found in caves. Foraging typically occurs over open water, along forest edges, and in clearings rather than in the dense interior of closed canopy.
species.where_to_look: Around sunset, watch over ponds and other open water and along edges where trees or shrubs meet open ground. Evening bats often work back and forth through the same feeding area, making them easier to follow against the sky.
species.when_to_see: Watch around dusk, when there is still enough light to see bats against the sky. Evening bats occur in Florida year-round, although activity drops on cold nights when fewer insects are flying.

size.length: About ten to eleven inches across the wings, with a body only a few inches long. It weighs roughly a quarter to half an ounce.
size.lifespan: Usually two to four years.

danger.people: Healthy evening bats avoid contact with people entirely. Like any wild mammal, a bat found on the ground or behaving abnormally during the day should not be handled with bare hands — bats are a potential rabies vector, and any bite warrants prompt medical evaluation.
danger.pets: A dog or cat that catches a grounded bat could receive a bite. Any pet with direct contact with a bat should be seen by a veterinarian. Keep pets away from bats found on the ground.

interaction.guidance: Watch foraging bats from a comfortable distance at dusk. Do not attempt to handle any bat, whether it appears healthy or not. If you find one on the ground or clinging to a low surface during daylight, do not touch it; alert park staff.

invasive.notes: Native throughout its range in eastern North America, including Florida. Not listed as invasive at any level.

conservation.status: Common across much of the southeastern United States and not listed as threatened in Florida. Loss of mature trees and other roost sites can reduce suitable habitat.

seasonality.note: Present all year, with activity following insect availability. Colder nights bring fewer bats out.

species.native_notes: Common and native throughout Florida (except the Keys) and the broader southeastern and eastern United States; listed as native to North America by FWC, Bat Conservation International, UF/IFAS, ADW, and Wikipedia citing IUCN.
species.teaser: Evening bats leave their roosts soon after sunset, often while enough light remains to watch them hunting over water and woodland edges.

how_it_lives.text: It comes out early, sometimes before the light has fully gone, and hunts in two bursts — one soon after dusk and another before dawn. The flight is slow and maneuverable, which suits picking insects out of cluttered air along a wood edge or over water.
They eat flying insects, especially beetles, along with moths, flies, mosquitoes and flying ants.

how_it_lives.label: A colony of relatives
how_it_lives.text: Females gather in maternity colonies to raise their young. Mothers recognize their own pups by scent and voice, although females have also been observed nursing pups that are not their own. Young males disperse; daughters may return to the colony where they were born.

species.plant_connections: Trees provide the daytime shelter these bats need. In Florida they roost in cavities and behind loose bark, and also use sheltered spaces at the bases of palm fronds. Keeping mature trees and standing dead wood supports the bats as well as the insects they feed on.

quick_hits: A raccoon's forepaws are unusually sensitive and dexterous. They use touch to search through mud, shallow water, leaf litter and cavities, often finding food where vision is little help.

Raccoons often manipulate food and other objects in water, which gave them the scientific name lotor, Latin for 'washer.' They are not simply cleaning their food: their highly sensitive forepaws are central to how they investigate objects and search for food.
Raccoons are capable problem-solvers and can learn how to open or manipulate unfamiliar objects. Experiments have also found that they can remember solutions to some tasks long after learning them.
Florida raccoons remain active year-round. Wetlands are especially good habitat, and raccoons forage along pond edges, marshes and coastal shorelines as well as in forests and developed areas.
species.range_and_origin: Native across much of North and Central America. Raccoons occur throughout Florida, from the Panhandle to the Keys, in wetlands, forests, coastal habitats and developed areas.

blocks.label: Size and build
blocks.text: A stocky mammal usually around the size of a small dog, with short front legs, longer hind legs and a bushy tail.

blocks.label: Facial mask
blocks.text: A black mask crosses the eyes, bordered by pale fur. Small rounded ears have pale edges.

blocks.label: Coat and tail
blocks.text: The coat is grizzled gray-brown, and the bushy tail has alternating dark and pale rings.

blocks.label: Paws
blocks.text: Each foot has five long toes. Front tracks look like small hands, while the longer hind footprints can resemble tiny human feet.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for the black facial mask and ringed tail. Even when the animal itself is hidden, five-toed tracks in soft mud near water can reveal where a raccoon has passed. Front tracks resemble small hands; hind tracks are longer.

species.diet: Raccoons eat whatever local conditions provide. Around water they take crabs, shellfish, frogs and other small animals. On land they eat insects, eggs, carrion, fruits and seeds. Around people they readily exploit pet food and unsecured garbage.
species.behavior: Raccoons are mainly nocturnal but may also be active around dawn, dusk or during the day. Adults usually forage alone; mothers travel with their young for months after the kits leave the den. They climb well and swim readily, and den in tree cavities, hollow logs, root tangles and sheltered spaces in buildings.
species.sounds: Raccoons make churring, chittering, growling and hissing sounds, but most animals encountered at a distance are quiet. Rustling vegetation or movement near water may reveal one first.
species.ecological_role: Raccoons are both predators and scavengers. They eat insects, crabs, frogs, eggs and other animal foods, and they also consume fruits and disperse some seeds in their droppings. Larger predators may take young raccoons.
species.habitat: Highly adaptable; in Florida, raccoons reach their highest natural densities in wetland-associated habitats — wooded swamps, mangrove edges, tidal marshes, and the borders of streams, ponds, and lakes. They also thrive in hardwood hammocks, suburban parks, golf courses, and urban greenways wherever trees and water are available. A reliable water source is the most consistent habitat requirement.
species.where_to_look: Look near ponds and other water, especially where vegetation provides cover and soft ground preserves tracks. Raccoons also use wooded edges and large trees with cavities. They are mostly active after dark, so tracks, scat or disturbed ground are often easier to find than the animal itself.
species.when_to_see: Raccoons live here year-round and are most active from dusk through the night. Daytime activity can also occur and does not by itself mean an animal is sick.

size.length: Usually about two to three feet from nose to tail and roughly eight to twenty pounds in Florida. Males tend to be larger.

danger.people: Keep your distance and never handle a raccoon. Raccoons can carry rabies, although being active during the day does not by itself indicate disease. Avoid any animal that is staggering, unusually aggressive, disoriented or approaching people without normal caution, and report it to park staff. Raccoon feces can also contain roundworm eggs that are hazardous if accidentally swallowed; do not touch raccoon scat or areas used repeatedly as latrines.
danger.pets: Keep pets away from raccoons. A cornered raccoon can seriously injure a dog or cat, and contact can expose pets to rabies or other diseases. Keep rabies vaccinations current and do not leave pet food outdoors.

interaction.guidance: Watch from a distance and never feed or approach a raccoon. Feeding teaches raccoons to associate people with food and increases the chance of conflicts. Keep food and trash secured. If a raccoon approaches closely or appears disoriented, move away and tell park staff.

conservation.status: Common and widespread in Florida and not a species of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Active year-round in southwest Florida. Females may be accompanied by young during part of the year, but raccoons can be encountered in any season.

species.teaser: Raccoons sometimes get into the park bins and cannot climb back out. We lower a plank; they climb up and sometimes pause at the top to look back — which we choose to read as thanks.

how_it_lives.text: Raccoons are mainly nocturnal but may also be active around dawn, dusk or during the day. Adults usually forage alone; mothers travel with their young for months after the kits leave the den.

Raccoons eat whatever local conditions provide. Around water they take crabs, shellfish, frogs and other small animals. On land they eat insects, eggs, carrion, fruits and seeds. Around people they readily exploit pet food and unsecured garbage.
They climb well and swim readily. Tree cavities, hollow logs, root tangles and sheltered spaces in buildings can all serve as dens.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Look near ponds and other water, especially where vegetation provides cover and soft ground preserves tracks. Raccoons also use wooded edges and large trees with cavities. They are mostly active after dark, so tracks, scat or disturbed ground are often easier to find than the animal itself.
Raccoons live here year-round and are most active from dusk through the night. Daytime activity can also occur and does not by itself mean an animal is sick.

where_to_find_it_here.label: In this park
where_to_find_it_here.text: The bins by the nursery are the reliable spot. Raccoons get in after dark and cannot climb the smooth sides to get back out, so a 2x4 stays leaning against the wall for them to walk up.

species.plant_connections: Raccoons eat the fruits of many Florida plants, including sea grape, beautyberry, cabbage palm, saw palmetto and persimmon. Seeds that survive digestion can be carried away from the parent plant in raccoon droppings. Large trees also provide cavities and sheltered places for daytime rest and dens.

quick_hits: The mite itself is essentially invisible — adults are roughly 0.2 mm long, about the width of a human hair. What visitors can actually see is its handiwork: patches of velvety, felt-like growth on lychee leaves called erinea.
Aceria litchii completes its entire life cycle in as little as 13 days under warm conditions, allowing populations to build rapidly on a single flush of new growth.

This is a genuine agricultural newcomer to Florida. The mite was first detected on the mainland United States in February 2018 at a lychee orchard on Pine Island, Lee County — and it has since spread to Manatee County and most other lychee-growing counties in the state.
Honey bees unwittingly help spread this mite. When bees forage on lychee flowers, mites hitch rides to new trees — a behavior called phoresy.
species.range_and_origin: Aceria litchii is native to Asia, where it has long been recorded as a serious pest of lychee in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Thailand, China, and Taiwan. It has spread well beyond its native range, establishing in Australia, Hawaii, Brazil, and more recently Europe. In the continental United States it is classified as a prioritized quarantine pest. The mite arrived in Florida in 2018 and has since spread across most lychee-producing counties in the state, including Manatee County. Its introduction to Florida is thought to involve plant material; DNA analysis suggests the Florida population may share a common origin with specimens from Taiwan.
more_information: The erineum is the mite's most remarkable feature — and its most visible one. When Aceria litchii feeds on a lychee leaf, its saliva triggers the leaf's own epidermal cells to produce abnormal trichomes (fine hairs) that pile up into a felted, velvety mat. The mites live, feed, and reproduce inside this structure, which shelters them from drying out and from many natural enemies.

Erinea pass through a color sequence that tells you something about the mite population within. Fresh erinea start white or nearly transparent; as the colony grows they shift to amber. Dark brown or black erinea are largely abandoned — the mites have overexploited that patch and moved on to the next flush of young growth elsewhere on the tree.

The mite's damage goes beyond leaf distortion. Heavy infestations reach flowers, stems, and developing fruit, reducing both yield and fruit quality. In Brazil, where the mite established in 2008, infestations caused an estimated 70 to 80 percent yield reduction in some growing areas — a figure that puts Florida's lychee industry, the largest in the continental U.S., in real economic jeopardy.

blocks.label: The mite itself
blocks.text: Adults are roughly 0.2 mm long — about the width of a human hair — translucent, cigar-shaped, and equipped with only four legs clustered near the head end. They cannot be seen without at least 20x magnification. In practice, you identify this species by its damage, not by spotting the animal.

blocks.label: Erinea on leaves
blocks.text: The primary sign is patches of abnormal, velvety or felt-like growth on lychee leaves, usually starting on the undersides. Fresh erinea are white to transparent; older ones turn amber. Dark brown patches indicate a spent colony that has moved on. Affected leaves often curl or become distorted.

blocks.label: Other plant parts
blocks.text: Erinea can also develop on petioles, stems, flower clusters, and young fruit. When multiple growth flushes are infested simultaneously, a tree can appear heavily mottled or deformed across much of its canopy.

blocks.label: Similar damage
blocks.text: Other mites and some fungi can cause superficially similar discoloration on lychee, but the distinctly felt-like texture of erinea — rather than simple spotting, scabbing, or powdery growth — is the key feature. If in doubt, a 20x hand lens will confirm the unusual hair structure.

identification.what_to_look_for: On any lychee tree in the park, scan the undersides of leaves for patches of velvety, felt-like growth. White to amber patches are active; dark brown ones are spent. Distorted or curled leaves, especially on young growth flushes, are another reliable clue. The mite itself is far too small to see without a microscope — the damage is the field mark.

species.diet: Aceria litchii feeds exclusively on lychee (Litchi chinensis). It uses needle-like mouthparts called stylets to pierce and feed on leaf epidermal cells, primarily on young leaves but also on flowers, petioles, stems, and developing fruit. It is highly host-specific and has not been documented feeding on other plants.
species.behavior: Mites live and breed inside the erinea they induce, which serve as both shelter and food source. Adults migrate from older, depleted erinea to fresh, young leaf and flower flushes, where they establish new erinea colonies. Within a tree, short-distance movement is ambulatory; longer-distance dispersal between trees relies primarily on wind, and phoresy on foraging honey bees has also been documented during the lychee flowering period. The life cycle from egg to adult takes as little as 13 days under warm conditions, with eggs hatching in 3 to 4 days.
species.sounds: Inaudible. Aceria litchii is a microscopic mite and produces no detectable sound.
species.ecological_role: As a host-specific plant feeder, Aceria litchii functions as an herbivore that can significantly reduce lychee tree productivity and alter canopy structure when populations are high. Predatory mites in the families Phytoseiidae and Stigmaeidae are documented natural enemies in its native Asian range and in other regions where it has established; whether an effective predator community has developed around Florida populations is an open question. Its role in the broader park food web is limited by its extreme host specificity.
species.habitat: Aceria litchii is restricted to lychee trees (Litchi chinensis). It thrives on trees with frequent flushes of young growth, which provide the fresh leaf tissue it needs to establish new erinea colonies. Warm, humid subtropical conditions — precisely those found in Manatee County — favor rapid population development.
species.where_to_look: Go directly to the lychee tree or trees in the park and examine the leaves, especially younger growth near branch tips. Flip leaves over and look for patches of velvety, felt-like growth on the undersides. You will not see the mites themselves without a microscope, but the erinea are often visible from arm's length once you know what to look for. Distorted or cupped young leaves are another quick cue to investigate further.
species.when_to_see: Erinea are present year-round on infested trees, but the most conspicuous damage appears on new growth flushes, which in South and Central Florida tend to be most abundant in spring and again in late summer and fall. Warm temperatures accelerate the mite's 13-day life cycle, so populations can spike rapidly after a flush of new growth.

size.length: Approximately 0.2 mm (about 1/120 inch) — invisible to the naked eye; a microscope is needed to see individual mites clearly
size.lifespan: Not well documented for this species; the full egg-to-adult cycle completes in as little as 13 days under warm conditions

danger.people: Aceria litchii poses no risk to people. It is a microscopic plant-feeding mite that neither bites nor stings humans and produces no toxins.
danger.pets: No risk to pets. This mite feeds exclusively on lychee plant tissue and has no capacity to affect animals.

interaction.guidance: There is no meaningful direct interaction — you cannot handle a mite this small. The best thing a visitor can do is observe the erinea damage on lychee leaves and report any new or spreading infestations to park staff, since this is an active quarantine pest in Florida.

invasive.notes: Aceria litchii is a non-native invasive pest, native to Asia and introduced to Florida no earlier than 2018. It is classified as a prioritized quarantine pest by federal and state authorities. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services established an eradication program and quarantine following its initial detection. It has since spread to Manatee County and most other lychee-producing counties in the state. Economic losses in other regions where it has established — up to 80 percent yield reduction — underscore the threat it poses to Florida's lychee industry.

conservation.status: Not a species of conservation concern. Aceria litchii is an introduced agricultural pest. No threatened or endangered listing applies, and management efforts aim to suppress or eradicate it rather than protect it.

seasonality.peak: spring and late summer–fall (coinciding with lychee growth flushes)
seasonality.note: Erinea are visible on infested lychee trees throughout the year. Mite populations build most rapidly during warm periods when the host tree produces new growth flushes, typically spring and again late summer through fall in Central Florida.

quick_hits: In warm climates, melon aphids can reproduce for long periods without mating. Females give birth to live female nymphs, which mature quickly and begin producing daughters of their own. Under favorable conditions, a newborn aphid can mature in about a week.
Melon aphids vary from pale yellow through green to nearly black, so color alone is unreliable. Look instead for the pair of dark tubes, called cornicles, projecting from the rear of the abdomen.
Ants often collect the sugary honeydew aphids excrete. In return, the ants may defend the colony from lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and other aphid enemies.
A swollen brown aphid that looks dry and papery may be a 'mummy.' A tiny parasitoid wasp developed inside it, killed it, and may eventually emerge through a round hole in the shell.
species.range_and_origin: Melon Aphids occur across tropical, subtropical and temperate regions worldwide. Their original geographic range is uncertain.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Tiny — usually around one-sixteenth of an inch long, with a soft, pear-shaped body. A hand lens or phone macro camera makes identification much easier.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Color varies widely, from pale yellow through yellow-green and olive to very dark green. Do not identify this species by color alone.

blocks.label: Cornicles
blocks.text: Two dark tubes called cornicles project from the rear of the abdomen. Their dark color is useful when identifying Melon Aphids, but other body features and the host plant may also be needed to confirm the species.

blocks.label: Winged and wingless forms
blocks.text: Most aphids in a settled colony are wingless. Crowding or declining plant quality can trigger production of winged females that disperse to new plants.

identification.what_to_look_for: Check the undersides of leaves and tender new shoots for clusters of tiny aphids. Sticky honeydew, black sooty mold or ants moving along the stems can reveal a colony before you notice the aphids themselves. With magnification, look for dark cornicles at the rear of the body. Brown, swollen aphid 'mummies' are evidence that parasitoid wasps have found the colony.

species.diet: Melon Aphids feed on phloem sap from a remarkably wide range of plants.
species.behavior: Aphids spend much of their time feeding in clusters. When a colony is disturbed, an alarm chemical can cause nearby aphids to move away or drop from the plant.
species.ecological_role: Melon Aphids feed lady beetles, lacewing larvae, flower-fly larvae and tiny parasitoid wasps. They can also spread plant viruses as they probe one plant after another, sometimes transmitting a virus even when they do not remain on the plant long enough to establish a colony.
species.habitat: Any landscape with soft-tissued host plants — gardens, vegetable patches, ornamental plantings, forest edges, roadsides, and disturbed areas supporting weedy hosts. The species thrives in warm, humid conditions and is well suited to Florida's climate year-round. Dense plantings and stressed or fertilizer-rich plants that produce abundant new growth tend to support the largest colonies.
species.where_to_look: Check tender new growth and the undersides of leaves, especially on hibiscus, citrus, peppers, cucumbers, melons and related plants. Ants traveling repeatedly up and down a stem may lead you to an aphid colony. Sticky honeydew or black sooty mold on leaves can also reveal aphids feeding above.
species.when_to_see: Melon Aphids can occur year-round in southwest Florida. Colonies build quickly when suitable plants are producing tender new growth and conditions favor reproduction.

size.length: Usually around one-sixteenth of an inch long.

danger.people: Harmless to people and pets. Melon Aphids feed on plants, not animals.

interaction.guidance: Look closely without handling the plant. A hand lens or phone camera can reveal the aphids, their dark cornicles, attendant ants and sometimes the papery remains of parasitized aphids.

invasive.notes: Melon Aphid is a widespread agricultural and horticultural pest in Florida. Colonies can damage tender growth and produce honeydew, and the species can transmit plant viruses among susceptible hosts.

conservation.status: Widespread and abundant; not a species of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Possible year-round in southwest Florida. Numbers can rise quickly when host plants produce tender new growth, then fall as plants change or predators, parasitoids and weather reduce the colony.

how_it_lives.text: Aphids cluster on tender shoots and the undersides of leaves, inserting slender mouthparts into the plant to reach sugar-rich phloem sap. Much of the excess sugar is excreted as sticky honeydew.
When a colony is disturbed, an alarm chemical can cause nearby aphids to move away or drop from the plant.

species.teaser: A colony can multiply without males. Females give birth to live daughters, and those daughters can begin producing young of their own within days.
species.plant_connections: Melon Aphids feed on an unusually broad range of plants. In Florida their hosts include cucumbers, melons and gourds; hibiscus and okra; citrus; peppers and eggplant; and many ornamentals and weeds. They concentrate on tender new growth and leaf undersides, where they tap into phloem sap. Heavy colonies can curl or distort young leaves, while their honeydew supports the black sooty mold often seen below an infestation.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Many aphid species look similar at this size. Body color alone is not enough to identify a Melon Aphid; close examination of body structures and the host plant may be needed for a confident identification.

species.teaser: Most carpenter ants in Florida do their foraging after dark. This one works the day shift — and it has been quietly spreading north through the state for decades.
quick_hits: Most Florida carpenter ants are nocturnal, but Camponotus planatus forages openly through the day, even in direct sun on surfaces hot enough to blister paint. It is far easier to spot than its larger relatives for exactly this reason.

This ant has been recorded nesting in epiphytic air plants — bromeliads wedged into the forks of trees — a nesting site unlike almost anything else a carpenter ant uses. Hollow branches, abandoned termite galleries, and the leaf axils of palms round out a remarkably varied toolkit.

At least four unrelated arthropods in Central America mimic Camponotus planatus so closely — matching its color, compact shape, and even the way it pumps its abdomen as it walks — that they can be nearly impossible to tell apart in the field.

The species first turned up in Florida records in Key West in 1887 and was long treated as a Keys specialist. It has since reached as far north as Jacksonville, and Manatee County sits squarely in its expanding range.
species.range_and_origin: Camponotus planatus is native to Cuba, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America as far as Colombia, and is considered native to parts of Texas as well. Florida's populations are regarded as introduced — the species was first recorded here in Key West in 1887 and appears to have spread substantially since 1980, now reaching as far north as Jacksonville. Its presence in Manatee County has been documented, and the colony you are looking at is part of that expanding foothold on Florida's west-central coast. Native status is debated for some parts of its range, but we treat this species as introduced to Florida.
more_information: Carpenter ants earned their name by excavating wood, but Camponotus planatus takes a less destructive approach. Rather than chewing out its own galleries, it moves into spaces that already exist — hollow branches, old termite tunnels, the tight axils where palm fronds meet the trunk. The work of finding a good void matters more than making one.

The colony tends aphids, scale insects, and other sap-suckers on nearby plants, collecting the honeydew they excrete. This is a common arrangement among ants, but C. planatus appears to take it seriously: workers have been observed guarding hemipteran colonies and driving off potential predators, protecting the sugar supply the way a rancher tends livestock.

Somewhere in Central America, four different arthropods — two spiders, a plant bug, and a mantid — have independently evolved to look and move like this ant. The mimicry in some cases extends to gait and the characteristic abdomen-pumping that ants use when walking. Being mistaken for a stinging or biting ant is apparently worth a lot of evolutionary effort.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Workers range from about an eighth to a quarter inch long — noticeably smaller than the Florida carpenter ant (Camponotus floridanus) they are often found near. Like most carpenter ants, colonies have minor and major workers; majors have proportionally larger heads.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Usually bicolored: the head and thorax are dark reddish-brown to dark red, and the abdomen (gaster) is black. Some individuals are nearly all black. The surface is not glossy — the body has a matte, slightly velvety look from short, dense hairs.

blocks.label: Shape and posture
blocks.text: Compact and relatively flat-bodied for a carpenter ant. The antennae are 12-segmented; the scape (first long segment) is longer than the width of the head. Workers move with the quick, purposeful gait typical of Camponotus — abdomen sometimes bobbing slightly.

blocks.label: Compared to similar species
blocks.text: Camponotus novogranadensis is the species most likely to cause confusion: both are small, dark, and matte-surfaced. C. planatus is distinguished by its reddish thorax contrasting with the black gaster; C. novogranadensis is uniformly black with yellowish-brown antennae and face markings.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a small, dark, fast-moving ant with a reddish thorax and black abdomen, active on tree trunks, branches, and shrub stems during the day. The daytime activity is the most reliable behavioral cue in Florida — if you see a compact dark carpenter ant moving around in full sun, C. planatus is a strong candidate. Check palm trunks and the bases of palm fronds, woody shrubs, and trees with rough bark or old termite damage.

species.diet: Honeydew collected from aphids, scales, and other sap-sucking insects is a primary food source; workers actively tend these insects on host plants. The colony also hunts and scavenges — taking small invertebrates and making use of whatever protein sources the foraging trail turns up. Like most carpenter ants, sweet liquid foods are especially sought after.
species.behavior: Foragers work during the day, including in direct sunlight — a notable contrast to Florida's other carpenter ant species, which are predominantly nocturnal. Workers travel singly or in loosely dispersed trails rather than tight columns. Nesting is opportunistic: the species prefers existing voids — hollow branches, old termite galleries, the leaf axils of palms, occasionally cavities in living trees or epiphytic bromeliads — rather than excavating fresh galleries. Colonies are headed by a single queen. New winged reproductives (alates) are produced from spring through fall, though the full details of their mating flights are not well documented for Florida populations.
species.sounds: Essentially silent. Like other ants, C. planatus communicates primarily through chemical signals — pheromones that mark trails, signal alarm, and coordinate nest activity. No sounds are detectable by a human observer.
species.ecological_role: As a predator and scavenger, the compact carpenter ant feeds on small invertebrates and helps break down dead wood through its nesting activities. Its mutualism with honeydew-producing hemipterans — tending aphids and scale insects in exchange for sugar — can protect pest populations on garden plants. Where it has become established in Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks it is a dominant ant and likely competes with native ant species for nest sites and food resources.
species.habitat: Primarily arboreal — most at home in trees and woody shrubs rather than on the ground. In Florida it favors tropical hardwood hammocks, palm plantings, and any landscape with mature woody vegetation offering hollow stems, loose bark, or old wood damage. It is also found in suburban and park settings wherever palms and ornamental trees provide suitable nesting cavities.
species.where_to_look: Check the trunks and lower branches of palms and broad-leaved trees, especially where bark is rough, loose, or shows old termite or wood-rot damage. Palm frond axils — the tight gap where a frond base meets the trunk — are a favored nest site. Also scan any plants with visible aphid or scale colonies; worker ants tending those insects are often C. planatus. Foragers move visibly during daylight hours, so a slow walk along the tree line with your eyes at bark level is the most productive approach.
species.when_to_see: Active year-round in Manatee County, with foraging visible during daylight throughout the day. Florida's mild winters do not interrupt activity, though warm months bring the most visible forager traffic. Winged reproductives appear from spring through fall.

size.length: About an eighth to a quarter inch (workers); minor workers toward the smaller end, major workers toward the larger
size.lifespan: Worker lifespan not well documented for this species; queens of related Camponotus species typically live several years

danger.people: Can bite if handled or if the nest is disturbed — the bite is a pinch rather than a sting, and no venom is injected. Under normal park conditions, foraging workers pay no attention to people.
danger.pets: No meaningful risk to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch foragers on tree bark from a few inches away — a phone macro or hand lens shows the bicolored body and busy antennae clearly. If you find a nest entrance, observe without probing; disturbed workers will bite. Replace any bark or debris you lift as you found it.

invasive.notes: Introduced to Florida and steadily expanding its range northward, C. planatus is now established across much of central and south Florida including Manatee County. It is not on Florida's official invasive species watch list, but it is documented as a competitor of native ant species, particularly in hardwood hammock habitats, and it tends pest hemipterans on landscape plants. Its spread appears to have accelerated since 1980, and climate change may facilitate further northward expansion.

conservation.status: Not assessed by IUCN. Abundant and expanding in Florida; no conservation concern.

seasonality.peak: warm months (April–October), when forager activity is highest
seasonality.note: Florida's climate allows continuous colony activity year-round. Winged reproductives are produced spring through fall. Daytime foraging makes this species visible whenever temperatures are warm.

species.internal_notes: Imported 2026-06-23 from iNaturalist observations (1 obs at PSBP).
quick_hits: Crane flies are often called Mosquito Hawks or Skeeter Eaters, but adults do not hunt mosquitoes. Despite the resemblance, they are harmless flies rather than giant mosquitoes.
Many crane flies look frustratingly similar, but Tipula furca has distinctly patterned wings with longitudinal brown and whitish markings.
The larvae live in wet debris and saturated soil along streams, hidden from view beneath the places where adults are found.

Like other true flies, a crane fly has one pair of functional wings. Behind them is a pair of small club-shaped structures called halteres, modified hind wings that help the insect sense rotation and stay balanced in flight.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America and documented in Florida. The species occurs in moist habitats where its larvae can develop in saturated soil and organic debris.
more_information: Many crane flies are difficult to identify to species from appearance alone. The patterned wings make Tipula furca more recognizable than some relatives, but a photograph may not always be enough for a certain identification.

blocks.label: Overall impression
blocks.text: A slender, long-legged crane fly with brownish coloring and distinctly patterned wings. The legs extend far beyond the body and often trail behind in flight.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: About half to three-quarters of an inch long, not counting the much longer legs.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: The wings have longitudinal brown and whitish markings rather than appearing uniformly clear. This pattern helps separate Tipula furca from many other crane flies.

blocks.label: Compared to mosquitoes
blocks.text: Crane flies are much larger and longer-legged than mosquitoes. They lack the mosquito's conspicuous piercing proboscis, and their wings do not have the covering of tiny scales found on mosquito wings.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for an extremely long-legged fly about half to three-quarters of an inch long. The best clue to this species is the wing pattern: longitudinal brown and whitish markings rather than plain clear wings. Its size and gangly proportions readily separate it from a mosquito.

species.diet: Larvae live among saturated soil and organic debris and feed on decaying material. Adult feeding in this species is poorly documented.
species.behavior: Adults are weak, long-legged fliers and often rest on vegetation. Their long legs can make flight look loose and unsteady.
species.ecological_role: The larvae help process decaying organic material in wet soil and debris. Crane flies also become food for many predators at both larval and adult stages.
species.habitat: Moist, vegetated areas near water — stream edges, pond margins, wet meadows, and spots where leaf litter or soil stays reliably damp and organic. Larvae favor the upper few centimeters of saturated soil or debris along watercourses. Adults are most reliably found where larval habitat is close at hand. In Florida, that translates to retention pond edges, shaded drainage corridors, and park areas with persistently moist soil under dense plantings.
species.where_to_look: Look around damp, vegetated areas, especially near pond margins, drainage areas and places where wet leaf litter accumulates. Adults may rest on low vegetation during the day and can also appear around lights.
species.when_to_see: Watch for adults around damp vegetation when conditions are humid. The seasonal timing of this species in southwest Florida is not well documented.

size.length: About half to three-quarters of an inch long, with legs extending much farther.

danger.people: Harmless to people. Crane flies do not sting, and this species does not have mosquito-like biting mouthparts or transmit mosquito-borne diseases.
danger.pets: No known risk to pets.

interaction.guidance: Watch without handling. Crane flies have very long, delicate legs that can be damaged easily.

invasive.notes: Native to North America and documented in Florida.

conservation.status: No specific conservation status has been identified for this species.

seasonality.note: Recorded at Palma Sola, but species-specific seasonal timing in southwest Florida is not well documented.

species.teaser: It looks like an oversized mosquito, but it does not bite. This is a crane fly, recognized by its long legs and distinctly striped wings.

how_it_lives.text: The larvae live out of sight in wet organic debris and saturated soil, including stream margins. There they feed among decomposing plant material.
Adults are long-legged, weak fliers and often rest on vegetation. They may also turn up around lights near damp habitat.

species.plant_connections: The plant connection is mostly below ground and after leaves fall. Larvae live in wet soil and organic debris, where they feed among decomposing leaves and other plant material. Moist leaf litter therefore supports an insect community that visitors rarely see.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Several other Tipula crane flies have similarly striped wings, including T. concava, T. eluta and T. strepens. A patterned wing can narrow the identification, but confirming T. furca may require details too small to judge in the field.

species.internal_notes: Imported 2026-06-23 from iNaturalist observations (2 obs at PSBP).
quick_hits: About 100 European Starlings were released in New York's Central Park in 1890 and 1891. That introduced population became established, and within decades starlings had spread across much of North America.

After the fall molt, fresh feathers have pale tips that give the bird a heavily spotted appearance. Through winter those tips gradually wear away, revealing the glossy green-and-purple breeding plumage underneath.

Starlings use a foraging technique called gaping. They push the closed bill into soil or leaf litter and then force it open, spreading the material apart to expose insects and other food hidden underneath.
Starlings are skilled mimics. Their long, varied songs can include imitations of other birds and sounds from their surroundings.
species.range_and_origin: Native to Europe and much of western and central Asia. Introduced populations are now widespread across North America and in several other parts of the world.
more_information: Large starling flocks sometimes form murmurations, with hundreds or thousands of birds turning together in shifting shapes before entering a communal roost. The tight flocking may make it harder for a predator to isolate one bird.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A stocky bird, about eight inches long, with a short tail and long pointed bill. On the ground it walks rather than hops. In flight, the wings look pointed and triangular.

blocks.label: Breeding plumage
blocks.text: Glossy black with green and purple iridescence that changes with the light. The bill becomes yellow in breeding plumage and the legs are pinkish.

blocks.label: Non-breeding plumage
blocks.text: After the fall molt, fresh feathers are tipped in white and buff, giving the bird a heavily speckled appearance. The bill darkens to gray-brown. As winter progresses and feather tips wear away, the speckles gradually disappear.

blocks.label: Juveniles
blocks.text: Young birds are plain gray-brown with a dark bill and can look very different from the adults around them. They begin acquiring spotted adult plumage later in their first year.

blocks.label: In flight
blocks.text: The short tail and pointed triangular wings give the bird a distinctive shape in flight. Wingbeats are rapid, often interrupted by short glides.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Often found alongside Common Grackles and other blackbirds, but starlings are stockier, shorter-tailed, and have a straight pointed bill rather than the curved bill of a grackle.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a stocky, short-tailed bird walking across lawns and probing the ground with a pointed bill. Adults are glossy and dark in spring and heavily spotted after the fall molt. Common Grackles are larger, longer-tailed and have heavier bills.

species.diet: They eat insects and other invertebrates, along with fruit, seeds and grain. Their diet shifts with what is available.
species.behavior: Starlings are highly social and commonly feed in groups. On lawns they usually walk quickly across the ground while searching and probing for food.
species.sounds: The song is a long mixture of whistles, rattles, warbles and harsher sounds. Starlings also imitate other birds, sometimes well enough to cause confusion about which species is calling.
species.ecological_role: Starlings eat insects, fruit and seeds and are themselves prey for hawks and other predators. Their more important ecological effect in North America comes from nesting: they use cavities and can compete with native cavity-nesting birds for limited nest sites.
species.habitat: Highly adaptable to almost any open or semi-open landscape — parks, lawns, agricultural fields, pastures, parking lots, suburban neighborhoods, and woodland edges. The common thread is access to short grass or bare ground for foraging and cavities (natural or artificial) for nesting. Dense, closed-canopy forest is avoided. Palma Sola's open lawn areas, garden beds, and tree lines are well within its preferred range.
species.where_to_look: Look on lawns, short grass and other open ground, where groups walk while probing for food. Starlings also use garden edges, parking areas and other developed spaces. Check trees and structures for birds entering cavities, and watch for flocks gathering toward evening.
species.when_to_see: Present in southwest Florida year-round. Starlings are active by day and often forage in groups on open ground.

size.length: About eight inches long, with a wingspan a little over a foot.

interaction.guidance: Watch without feeding or approaching a nest. Starlings readily use lawns and other developed areas, so they can often be observed from paths.

invasive.notes: European Starlings are introduced and invasive in North America. They compete with native cavity-nesting birds for nest sites and can cause agricultural damage when large flocks concentrate around crops or livestock operations. The species is now widespread and firmly established.

conservation.status: European Starlings remain abundant and widespread in North America and are not considered threatened. Their North American population has declined substantially from its late twentieth-century peak.

seasonality.note: Present year-round in southwest Florida. Flock size and local abundance can vary through the year.

species.teaser: Its winter spots disappear without a molt. The pale tips simply wear off its feathers, revealing glossy green and purple plumage underneath.

how_it_lives.text: Starlings are highly social and commonly feed in groups. On lawns they usually walk quickly across the ground while searching and probing for food.
They eat insects and other invertebrates, along with fruit, seeds and grain. Their diet shifts with what is available.

species.plant_connections: Starlings feed on many fruits and seeds as well as insects found in lawns and soil. Trees also provide nesting and roosting sites, especially where trunks contain natural cavities or old woodpecker holes.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Larger and longer-tailed than a European Starling, with a heavier bill. A starling has a compact body, short tail and more pointed wings.

species.internal_notes: Imported 2026-06-23 from iNaturalist observations (1 obs at PSBP).
quick_hits: Instead of trapping prey in a web, a spitting spider shoots a sticky mixture from its fangs that pins a small animal to the surface. The spider then moves in to bite.
The unusually high, rounded front of the body houses enlarged glands involved in producing the spider's sticky prey-catching fluid.
Spitting spiders have six eyes arranged in three pairs rather than the eight eyes found in many familiar spiders.
It is a slow hunter. Rather than chasing fast prey, it approaches within range and immobilizes the target before closing in.
A female carries her egg sac beneath her body, held in her mouthparts, rather than leaving it attached to a web.
species.range_and_origin: A tropical species now found widely around the world, often in and around buildings. It is introduced and established in Florida.

blocks.label: Size and shape
blocks.text: A small brown spider about a quarter-inch long, with long slender legs and a conspicuously high, rounded front body section.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Brown to chestnut overall, with darker mottling on the rounded front of the body and patterned markings across the abdomen.

blocks.label: Eyes
blocks.text: Six small eyes are arranged in three pairs. This can help confirm a spitting spider in a close photograph, but the eyes are difficult to see without magnification.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Other spitting spiders can look very similar. The high rounded front of the body and six-eye arrangement help identify the family, but confirming Scytodes fusca may require a close photograph or specialist examination.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look for a small mottled-brown spider with long thin legs and an unusually high, rounded front body section. During the day it may rest on a wall, beneath an overhang or in another sheltered spot. The six eyes are useful only in a close photograph.

species.diet: Small insects and other spiders. The sticky attack allows a relatively slow-moving spider to immobilize prey before approaching closely.
species.behavior: It hunts on foot rather than building a prey-catching web. Most activity occurs at night; by day it often rests in a sheltered place. The spider approaches prey slowly rather than chasing it.
species.ecological_role: A predator of small insects and other spiders in sheltered habitats. It in turn can be eaten by larger spiders, lizards and other small predators.
species.habitat: Strongly associated with warm, sheltered, low-humidity spaces: the interiors and exterior walls of buildings, covered walkways, greenhouses, garden sheds, and similar structures. Outdoors it favors surfaces beneath overhangs, inside hollow trees, under loose bark, and among dense ground debris. It is a synanthropic species — one that thrives alongside human habitation — and is rarely found far from some form of cover.
species.where_to_look: Check sheltered surfaces such as the undersides of benches, covered structures, exterior walls, beneath overhangs and under loose bark. During the day the spider may remain motionless in a protected corner; it hunts after dark.
species.when_to_see: Most active at night. During the day it may be found resting in sheltered places. Florida's warm climate allows activity through much of the year, but Palma Sola has too few records to establish a local seasonal pattern.

size.length: About a quarter-inch long, not counting the legs.

danger.people: Not considered medically significant to people. This small spider is not aggressive and normally retreats or remains still when disturbed. Avoid handling it.
danger.pets: No known meaningful risk to pets.

interaction.guidance: Observe without touching or handling. A resting spider can be photographed where it is without disturbing its shelter.

invasive.notes: Introduced and established in Florida. It is not currently treated as a major invasive species or management concern.

conservation.status: Widespread globally and not known to be of conservation concern.

seasonality.note: Established in Florida and potentially present year-round in sheltered habitat. Palma Sola records are too limited to estimate local frequency or seasonality.

species.teaser: A female carries her egg sac beneath her body in her mouthparts instead of leaving it attached to a web.

how_it_lives.text: It hunts on foot rather than building a prey-catching web. Most activity occurs at night; by day it often rests in a sheltered place.
The spider approaches prey slowly rather than chasing it. Once a small animal is immobilized, the spider moves in to bite and feed.

species.plant_connections: Outdoors, spitting spiders can shelter under loose bark, inside tree cavities and among dense plant debris. Plants provide cover and hunting surfaces rather than food; the spider itself is entirely predatory.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Other Scytodes look very similar. The high rounded front of the body and the six-eye arrangement identify the family, but confirming Scytodes fusca may require a close photograph or specialist examination.

species.internal_notes: Imported 2026-06-23 from iNaturalist observations (1 obs at PSBP).
quick_hits: Adult paper wasps drink nectar, but their larvae are fed animal prey. Workers hunt caterpillars and other soft-bodied insects, chew them up and carry the food back to the nest.
Paper wasps scrape fibers from weathered wood and dead plant stems, chew them into pulp and use the material to build their nest.
Unlike a hornet or yellowjacket nest, a paper-wasp nest has no enclosing paper shell. The open cells remain visible, usually facing downward beneath a sheltered attachment point.
A female can begin a nest herself. After the first workers mature, they take over much of the foraging, nest building and defense.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, including Florida and the Gulf Coast.
