how_it_lives.text: A slow, methodical forager that works the interior branches of tall trees, pausing at every perch to look above and below before moving on. Nothing hurried about it.
Mostly insects gleaned from bark, twigs and foliage — caterpillars, moths, butterflies, beetles, leafhoppers, aphids, cicadas, dragonflies — plus berries, especially in fall on migration.

It migrates at night. In winter it holds a solo feeding territory and drives off other yellow-throated vireos, while still travelling with mixed flocks of other species. Both parents share the incubating and the feeding.

quick_hits: The only North American warbler that forages like a nuthatch, creeping up, down, and sideways along tree trunks and thick limbs to probe bark crevices for hidden insects — no other warbler in the family regularly works the bark this way.

Built for it: the Black-and-white Warbler has an unusually long hind toe and claw — nearly as long as its entire leg — plus shortened tarsi and a long, slightly curved bill, all evolved for gripping bark and probing deep into crevices.
Its song is a thin, high-pitched, repetitive weesy-weesy-weesy, famously likened to a squeaky wheelbarrow. Once you learn it, you will recognize this bird by ear long before you spot it on the trunk.
Its genus name Mniotilta means 'moss-plucking' — a nod to how it picks prey from mossy, lichened bark. Despite spending almost all its time high on trunks, it nests directly on the ground.
species.range_and_origin: The Black-and-white Warbler breeds across eastern and central North America, from the Northwest Territories south to Texas and the Carolinas. It winters in Florida, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America as far as Peru. Florida serves as one of its northernmost regular wintering grounds, and this species is among the earliest fall migrants to arrive — sometimes appearing as early as mid-August — and among the first to push north again in spring.
more_information: What sets this bird apart from every other warbler in North America is its nuthatch-like foraging style. It creeps up, down, and around tree trunks and major limbs on specialized feet — an unusually long hind toe and claw, roughly as long as the tarsus itself, and shortened legs that keep its center of gravity low against the bark.
Unlike a woodpecker, it does not brace with its tail; it relies entirely on those gripping feet.

The long, slightly curved bill is adapted for probing into bark fibers and crevices, where it targets caterpillars, bark beetles, wood borers, ants, flies, spiders, and other arthropods. Because it hunts dormant and pupating insects tucked inside bark rather than active flying bugs, it can move through on migration earlier in spring than most leaf-gleaning warblers.

Despite logging almost all of its waking hours on vertical surfaces, the Black-and-white Warbler nests at ground level — placing its open cup of leaves, grass stems, bark strips, and pine needles at the base of a tree, stump, rock, or log, or in a small depression in the forest floor. The female handles incubation alone for 10 to 12 days; both parents feed the young.
The oldest banded individual on record lived 11 years and 3 months.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A boldly pin-striped black-and-white warbler about the size of a chickadee, with a flat head, long wings, and a slightly downcurved bill. Its creeping behavior on tree trunks is its best field mark — no other warbler does this routinely.

blocks.label: Male vs. Female
blocks.text: Adult males have a black throat and a solid black cheek patch, giving them a bandit-mask look. Females and immatures show a white to cream throat and a grey or buffy cheek — paler overall, with less bold streaking on the flanks.

blocks.label: Possible Confusion
blocks.text: The Blackpoll Warbler is also black and white but sports a solid black cap and never creeps on trunks. The tree-creeping behavior of the Black-and-white is the clincher — if it is working the bark, it is this species.

identification.what_to_look_for: Scan the trunks and thick limbs of mature trees rather than the outer foliage. Watch for a small, hyperactive bird moving in zigzag spirals around the bark — up, down, and sideways — rather than hopping branch to branch. Bold black-and-white stripes run head to tail; the striped crown with a white central stripe is visible even at a distance.

species.diet: Primarily insects and spiders gleaned from tree bark: caterpillars (including moth and butterfly larvae), bark beetles, wood borers, ants, flies, leafhoppers, aphids, and daddy longlegs. Occasionally catches insects on the wing or visits sapsucker holes for insects attracted to the sap.
species.behavior: Creeps up, down, and sideways along tree trunks and major limbs in a spiraling, zigzagging path — the only North American warbler to forage on bark this way. Unlike the Brown Creeper, which only climbs upward, this species works in any direction. It switches its body side to side at each hop while foraging. Males defend winter territories aggressively, sometimes driving off other species.
species.sounds: The song is a thin, high-pitched, repetitive weesy-weesy-weesy — a series of wee-see phrases repeated six or more times in a chanting rhythm, famously compared to a squeaky wheelbarrow. The absence of a complex ending helps separate it from other high-pitched warbler songs. Both sexes give a sharp chit or pit call; a softer seet-seet flight call is also heard.
species.ecological_role: A specialist insect predator of bark-dwelling and wood-boring invertebrates — a foraging niche almost no other songbird occupies in Florida's winter woodland. By targeting pupae, larvae, and dormant insects inside bark, it complements foliage-gleaning warblers rather than competing with them, and helps suppress pest insect populations in mature tree stands.

size.length: 4.3 to 5.1 inches; wingspan 7.1–8.7 inches; weight 0.3–0.5 oz
size.lifespan: Typically several years; the oldest banded individual on record reached 11 years and 3 months.

species.habitat: Mature and second-growth deciduous or mixed woodland; also found in parks, riparian corridors, and suburban areas with large trees during migration and winter. In Florida's winter, it uses a wide range of wooded habitats including mangroves, oak hammocks, and tree-lined parks.
species.where_to_look: Scan the rough bark of mature oaks and other large native trees in the park's mid-story and canopy. Look at the trunk and main limbs, not the leaf tips — this bird works the bark, not the foliage. It often forages surprisingly low on the trunk, so check at eye level as well as overhead.
species.when_to_see: Active during daylight hours year-round during its Florida stay. Fall arrivals can appear as early as mid-August; numbers build through October and peak in winter. Spring departure begins by March, with most birds gone by late April. Best detected by its squeaky weesy song on cool, still mornings when sound carries well through the trees.

seasonality.note: Winter visitor.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: It creeps along trunks and heavy limbs in a spiraling, zigzag path, working up, down and sideways — the only North American warbler that forages on bark this way. A brown creeper only goes up; this one goes any direction, switching which side of its body leads at each hop.

Insects and spiders taken off the bark: caterpillars, bark beetles, wood borers, ants, flies, leafhoppers, aphids, daddy longlegs. It will occasionally catch something in the air, or visit a sapsucker's holes for the insects the sap has drawn.
Males defend winter territories hard, sometimes driving off other species entirely.

quick_hits: A tiny, jewel-toned warbler — blue-gray above with a bright yellow throat and breast, a yellow-green patch on the back, bold white eye crescents, and a distinctive chestnut-and-black breast band most vivid on adult males.

Its nest is an architectural marvel: the female burrows into a hanging clump of Spanish moss, hollows out a chamber from the inside, and lines it with fine grass and hair — a hidden pouch invisible from below.
It forages acrobatically, often hanging upside down at the very tips of branches to snatch caterpillars and spiders tucked beneath leaves — a trick shared by few other warblers.
Its song is instantly recognizable: a rising, accelerating buzzy trill that pinches off with a sharp zip at the end — often described as sounding like a tiny zipper being yanked open.
species.range_and_origin: The Northern Parula breeds across eastern North America from southeastern Canada south through the eastern United States, with its southern breeding limit running roughly through northern Florida around the latitude of Lake Okeechobee. In the Bradenton area and across much of peninsular Florida, it is primarily a migrant and winter visitor, arriving in fall and departing by spring. A small number of pairs breed in northern Florida, and rare nesting records exist as far south as Collier and Palm Beach counties, but the species is not a regular summer resident this far south.
more_information: The Northern Parula's fate is tightly bound to epiphytes. In the South, it nests almost exclusively within hanging clumps of Spanish moss (Tillandsia usneoides), where the female hollows out the interior, forms a cup near the bottom, and lines it with soft fibers and hair. The finished nest is all but invisible — detectable only by watching the comings and goings of the parents.

Despite its size — barely larger than a hummingbird — this warbler is a persistently vocal presence. Males sing well into the nesting season, even while feeding young. The song, a buzzy ascending trill that ends with an abrupt zip, is one of the more distinctive sounds in Florida's oak hammocks during winter and migration.

Northern Parulas have increased by over 1% per year from 1966 to 2019 — a cumulative gain of roughly 47% — according to the North American Breeding Bird Survey. Partners in Flight estimates the global breeding population at 18 million individuals, making this one of the more encouraging warbler success stories.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A hyperactive, canopy-loving warbler roughly 4.3 to 4.7 inches long. Blue-gray above with a mossy-green back patch, two white wing bars, a bright yellow throat and breast, a white belly, and broken white eye crescents. Adult males wear a sharp chestnut-and-black breast band; females and immatures are paler and may lack the band entirely.

blocks.label: Seasonal Tips
blocks.text: In fall and winter look for the telltale broken white eye crescents, which persist even on dull non-breeding birds. In spring, listen for the bzzzzz-zip song from the live oak canopy — a singing male is often easier to hear than to see. During migration, birds can drop lower into the mid-story, giving better looks than their usual treetop haunts.

identification.what_to_look_for: Scan the mid-to-upper canopy of live oaks and other mature trees, especially where Spanish moss is draped. Watch for a very small, restless bird fluttering at branch tips or hanging upside down to glean insects. The broken white eye crescents are the most reliable field mark in all plumages — no other eastern warbler combines them with yellow underparts and a blue-gray back.

species.diet: Primarily insects and spiders, including caterpillars, beetles, flies, ants, and scale insects gleaned from leaves and branch tips. On wintering grounds the diet occasionally includes small berries, seeds, or nectar.
species.behavior: An acrobatic, hyperactive canopy forager — it hops rapidly through branches, hovers briefly at leaf clusters, and frequently hangs upside down at twig tips to reach hidden prey. During migration it joins mixed-species warbler flocks; on the breeding grounds it travels alone or in pairs. Males sing persistently from the canopy, often even while feeding nestlings.
species.sounds: The signature song is a rising, buzzy trill that accelerates and pinches off with a sharp, abrupt zip — often rendered as bzzzzz-zip and likened to a miniature zipper. A second song type consists of two or more bouts of buzzy notes separated by brief pauses. Both sexes give a sharp chip call while foraging or during aggressive interactions.
species.ecological_role: A specialist predator of canopy arthropods — caterpillars, beetles, flies, and spiders — helping suppress populations of herbivorous insects in mature forest and hammock canopies. It also serves as prey for small raptors and other mesopredators, linking the insect and vertebrate layers of the food web.

size.lifespan: up to at least 5 years 11 months recorded in the wild (banding data)

species.habitat: During the breeding season, mature moist woodland draped with Spanish moss or beard lichens, often near water. Outside the breeding season it becomes a habitat generalist, turning up in nearly any wooded setting — parks, shade trees, scrubby edges, and overgrown gardens — during migration and winter.
species.where_to_look: Focus on the mid-to-upper canopy of the park's mature live oaks, particularly where Spanish moss grows in abundance near the wetland margins and shaded hammocks. Listen for the bzzzzz-zip song first — the bird is usually easier to hear than to see. Bring binoculars and be prepared for "warbler neck"; they rarely come low.
species.when_to_see: Present in the Bradenton area primarily from October through April as a migrant and winter visitor. Peak activity occurs during fall migration (September to October) and spring migration (March to April), when birds are most numerous and males are most vocal. Winter residents can be found quietly foraging through the canopy on any cool morning from November through February.

seasonality.note: Migrant and winter visitor.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Population has grown roughly 47% since 1966; global breeding population estimated at 18 million individuals.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: Hyperactive and acrobatic in the canopy — it hops rapidly along branches, hovers at leaf clusters, and hangs upside down at twig tips to reach what is underneath.
Insects and spiders: caterpillars, beetles, flies, ants, scale insects gleaned from leaves and branch tips. On the wintering grounds it will also take small berries, seeds or nectar.
On migration it joins mixed warbler flocks; on the breeding grounds it is alone or in a pair, and the males sing persistently from the canopy, often while feeding nestlings.

quick_hits: Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest the waxy fruits of bayberries and wax myrtles, foods many other birds cannot use efficiently. That extra winter food helps them remain farther north than most other warblers.
Unlike many warblers that search mainly for insects in foliage, Yellow-rumped Warblers also catch insects in flight, forage on the ground and switch heavily to fruit during winter.
The birds seen in Florida are usually the white-throated 'Myrtle' form. Farther west, the 'Audubon's' form has a yellow throat.
The birds at Palma Sola are winter visitors. They breed far to the north and leave Florida again in spring.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Yellow-rumped Warblers breed mainly across Canada, Alaska and parts of the northern United States, then move south for winter. Florida is wintering habitat rather than breeding habitat.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: A sturdy warbler about five and a half inches long, with a fairly large head and a narrow tail.

blocks.label: Winter plumage
blocks.text: Winter birds are gray-brown above and pale below, with streaking on the breast and sides. Look for the bright yellow rump, small yellow patches along the sides, a white throat and two pale wing bars.

blocks.label: Spring males
blocks.text: By spring, males can become much more strongly patterned in gray, black and white, while retaining the yellow rump and side patches.

blocks.label: Similar species
blocks.text: Palm Warblers are also common Florida winter visitors but usually forage lower and repeatedly bob or wag the tail.

identification.what_to_look_for: Look first for the yellow rump, often easiest to see when the bird flies. Winter birds also show a white throat, yellow patches along the sides and two pale wing bars. Listen for a short, flat check call from shrubs and trees.

species.diet: Insects and other small arthropods are important during the breeding season. In winter, fruit becomes a major food source, including wax myrtle, bayberry, poison ivy, grapes and other berries.
species.behavior: Yellow-rumped Warblers forage at several heights, searching foliage and bark, catching insects in short flights and sometimes feeding on the ground. They migrate at night.
species.sounds: The most useful sound in Florida is a short, flat check call, often given while the bird is foraging or flying. The male's breeding song is a soft series of whistled notes, but visitors here are much more likely to hear the call.
species.ecological_role: Yellow-rumped Warblers eat insects during much of the year and consume large quantities of fruit in winter. Seeds from some fruits can pass through the bird and be carried away from the parent plant.
species.plant_connections: Wax myrtle is especially important winter food. Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest its wax-coated fruits, helping them survive when insects are scarce. They also eat fruits from poison ivy, grapes and other woody plants, making fruiting shrubs and vines important winter habitat.

size.length: About five and a half inches long.

species.habitat: Breeds in mature coniferous and mixed coniferous-deciduous forests in the far north. In winter — the only time it occurs in Florida — it occupies a wide range of open habitats: woodland edges, shrubby thickets, coastal vegetation, parks, residential areas, dunes with bayberry or wax myrtle, and even open beaches. One of the most habitat-flexible warblers in North America.
species.where_to_look: Check fruiting wax myrtles and other shrubs, especially during winter. Birds also forage through tree canopies and along woodland edges, sometimes flying out from a branch to catch an insect. Listen for the short check call when a flock is moving through.
species.when_to_see: A winter visitor to Florida, generally present from fall into spring. Palma Sola records are still too few to define a local peak.

seasonality.note: Winter visitor to Florida. Recorded at Palma Sola, but local observations are too few to establish how regularly it occurs in the park.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and avoid disturbing birds feeding in fruiting shrubs.

invasive.notes: Native North American species and a natural seasonal visitor to Florida. Not invasive.

conservation.status: Widespread and not currently considered threatened.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Palm Warblers are also common Florida winter visitors but usually forage lower and repeatedly bob or wag the tail. Yellow-rumped Warblers show the bright yellow rump that gives the species its name.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: Yellow-rumped Warblers forage at several heights, searching foliage and bark, catching insects in short flights and sometimes feeding on the ground. They migrate at night.
Their diet changes with the season. Insects dominate during the breeding season, while fruit becomes especially important in winter.

species.teaser: Watch the bird as it flies away. The flash of yellow above the tail often identifies a Yellow-rumped Warbler before you get a good look at anything else.

quick_hits: A sharp-looking gray-and-white warbler with a vivid yellow throat, bold black mask, and long white eyebrow stripe. Two white wingbars and black streaks along the flanks complete the field mark set.
Forages more like a nuthatch than a typical warbler — creeping methodically along branches and probing bark crevices, pine cones, and needle clusters with a notably long, pointed bill.
One of the earliest warblers to return in spring, often arriving before leaves emerge. In Florida winters, watch for them probing the fronds high in palm crowns.
Early naturalist Mark Catesby called it the Yellow-throated Creeper — a name that still fits perfectly today.
The oldest confirmed wild individual lived at least 6 years and 10 months — a male banded in Alabama in 2012 and spotted again in Ohio in 2018, well beyond the species' typical lifespan.
species.range_and_origin: The Yellow-throated Warbler breeds across the southeastern United States from southern Pennsylvania and northern Missouri south to the Gulf Coast and into central Florida. Three subspecies are recognized; one of them, S. d. stoddardi, is a non-migratory resident of the Florida Panhandle and north-central Florida. Elsewhere in the state, the species is primarily a winter visitor, with birds also passing through during fall and spring migration. The wintering range extends along the Gulf Coast into eastern Mexico, the Caribbean, and northern Central America.
more_information: The Yellow-throated Warbler is built for bark — its bill is longer and stouter than that of most warblers, and it uses that bill to pry into crevices, pine cones, and clusters of pine needles in search of beetles, moths, caterpillars, flies, and spiders.
It spends the majority of its time in the outer half of high canopy branches, creeping and probing with deliberate, unhurried movements unlike the restless flitting of most warblers.

In Florida winters, the species shifts its focus to palm trees, working the crowns and probing among the fronds with the same methodical technique it uses on pine and cypress during the breeding season. It will also hawk for flying insects in warmer weather and forage on insects drawn to flowering palms and agave.

Nests are placed high in the canopy — often tucked into curtains of Spanish moss or woven from bark strips, grasses, and plant down near the outer tips of branches in pine, cypress, or live-oak trees. The female builds the nest and incubates a clutch of three to five eggs for about twelve to thirteen days. Pairs commonly raise two broods per season.

Sharp-eyed visitors have a subtle field challenge worth attempting: the three subspecies differ in one small but telling detail. Birds of the eastern subspecies (S. d. dominica) usually show a touch of yellow at the very front of the white eyebrow stripe — right above the lore — while birds of the Midwestern albilora subspecies always show a purely white supercilium all the way to the bill.
The difference is small, but it rewards a careful second look through binoculars.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A slender, long-billed warbler with a brilliant yellow throat, white underparts, and plain gray upperparts. Bold black mask, a long white eyebrow stripe, a white neck patch, and two crisp white wingbars. Black streaks run along the flanks.

blocks.label: Bill and Body
blocks.text: Compared with other warblers, the body is slightly heavier and the bill noticeably longer and thicker — a key structural clue even at distance. The tail is blunt and only slightly notched.

blocks.label: Sexes and Ages
blocks.text: Males and females look alike at a glance, but females and first-year birds are somewhat duller, with less intense black on the face and slightly washed-out flanks.

blocks.label: Similar Species
blocks.text: No other eastern warbler combines a bright yellow throat with gray-and-white plumage. The Blackburnian Warbler shows yellow on the throat but has a yellow — not white — eyebrow stripe and pale back streaks.

identification.what_to_look_for: In winter and early spring (November through March), scan the undersides of palm fronds and the coarse bark of mature pines for a tiny gray-and-white bird creeping deliberately along limbs rather than flitting — the yellow throat glows like a lantern even in dappled shadow. During the breeding season and spring migration, listen for a loud, sweet, descending whistle drifting down from the highest pine or cypress canopy; singing birds will often perch at the very tip of an exposed branch. Year-round, the long bill is visible the moment the bird leans into a bark crevice or needle cluster — no other warbler in the park probes quite like that.

species.diet: Primarily insects and spiders — beetles, moths, caterpillars, grasshoppers, crickets, flies, mosquitoes, ants, scale insects, and aphids. In winter in Florida, they also forage on insects attracted to flowering palms.
species.behavior: Moves deliberately through the high canopy, creeping along branches and leaning trunks like a nuthatch rather than flitting. Probes bark crevices, pine cones, and needle clusters with its long bill, and will also launch short aerial sallies to catch flying insects. One of the earliest warbler migrants in spring, often arriving before leaf-out.
species.sounds: Song is a melodic, descending series of clear whistled notes that accelerates and then rises abruptly on the final note — often rendered as teeew-teeew-teeew-tew-tew-twi. Frequently delivered from a high, exposed perch in the canopy. Call is a sharp, strong chirp.
species.ecological_role: An insect predator that targets bark-dwelling and canopy insects often overlooked by other birds. By foraging in pine cones, needle clusters, and bark crevices, it suppresses pests such as scale insects, beetles, and caterpillars that can damage trees. It also serves as prey for woodland raptors and larger predators.

size.lifespan: typically 3–4 years in the wild; the oldest confirmed individual reached at least 6 years and 10 months (banded in Alabama 2012, resighted in Ohio 2018)

species.habitat: Pine forests with open understories, bald cypress swamps, live-oak woodlands draped in Spanish moss, and riverine bottomlands with large sycamores. In Florida winters, also found in palm groves and mixed woodlands in parks and gardens.
species.where_to_look: Scan the upper canopy of the park's taller trees — pines, live oaks, and palms are all worth checking. Birds spend most of their time on the outer portions of high branches, so binoculars aimed upward are essential. During migration or on cold mornings, individuals occasionally drop lower, making a closer look possible.
species.when_to_see: Present in the Bradenton area primarily from fall through early spring as a winter resident, with peak activity November through March. A small non-migratory population resides year-round in north and north-central Florida. Most active and vocal during daylight hours; migrants travel mostly at night.

seasonality.presence: winter resident; year-round in parts of north/north-central Florida
seasonality.note: A non-migratory subspecies (S. d. stoddardi) resides year-round in the Florida Panhandle. In the Bradenton area, birds are most reliably seen November through March; spring and fall migrants may pass through in April and October.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy. Because Yellow-throated Warblers are canopy specialists, tracking one through the treetops can quickly earn you a sore neck — what birders affectionately call warbler neck. Stay on established pathways so you can safely keep your eyes on the canopy, and avoid stepping into garden beds or native understory plantings while looking up.

conservation.status: Least Concern (IUCN). Population estimated at roughly two million individuals and currently expanding its breeding range northward. Habitat loss — particularly of mature pine and cypress forests — remains the primary long-term concern.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: It moves deliberately through the high canopy, creeping along branches and leaning trunks more like a nuthatch than a warbler, and probes bark crevices, pine cones and needle clusters with that long bill. It will also sally out after flying insects.
Insects and spiders — beetles, moths, caterpillars, grasshoppers, crickets, flies, mosquitoes, ants, scale insects, aphids. In Florida winters it works the insects drawn to flowering palms.
One of the earliest warblers back in spring, often arriving before the leaves are out.

quick_hits: The Cape May Warbler has an unusually shaped, semitubular tongue that helps it drink nectar from flowers and juice from fruit.
The scientific name tigrina refers to the dark streaks across the male's yellow breast.
On its northern breeding grounds, Cape May Warbler numbers rise when spruce budworms become abundant. In years with abundant food, females can lay unusually large clutches for a warbler.
Florida is mostly a stop along the journey. Most Cape May Warblers continue across the Caribbean to their wintering grounds.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America and the Caribbean region. Cape May Warblers breed in boreal forests across Canada and the northern United States, migrate through Florida, and winter mainly in the Caribbean.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Breeding males have yellow underparts heavily streaked with black, a chestnut cheek patch, dark eyestripe and a large white patch in the wing.

blocks.label: Female and nonbreeding
blocks.text: Females and immature birds are much duller, usually gray-olive above and pale yellowish below with fine streaking. A yellowish rump, short tail and slightly downcurved bill can help with identification.

blocks.label: Confusion species
blocks.text: Dull birds can resemble other migrating warblers. Cape May Warblers have a relatively short tail, fine streaking across the breast and sides, and a slender bill that curves slightly downward. Palm Warblers repeatedly pump the tail; Yellow-rumped Warblers show a brighter yellow rump.

identification.what_to_look_for: In spring, look for a yellow bird with heavy dark breast streaking and a chestnut cheek patch. Duller birds are harder: look for the short tail, streaked underparts and slightly downcurved bill. Cape May Warblers often forage high in trees, so a clear view may take patience.

species.diet: Insects dominate on the breeding grounds, especially spruce budworm caterpillars when they are abundant. During migration and winter, Cape May Warblers also drink flower nectar and fruit juice.
species.behavior: Cape May Warblers usually forage high in trees, picking insects from foliage and branch tips and sometimes flying out to catch insects in the air. Migration occurs mostly at night. Outside the breeding season they also visit flowers for nectar and may defend productive flowering plants from other nectar feeders.
species.sounds: The song is a very high, thin series of repeated notes. The call is a soft, high sip. The song can be difficult to hear for people who have lost sensitivity to high frequencies.
species.ecological_role: Cape May Warblers are important predators of spruce budworm caterpillars on their northern breeding grounds. During migration and winter they also feed at flowers, putting them in direct contact with pollen as they drink nectar.
species.plant_connections: This warbler changes its relationship with plants through the year. In northern spruce forests it searches needles and branch tips for spruce budworm caterpillars. During migration and winter it also visits flowers for nectar and punctures fruit for juice. Flowering trees and shrubs can therefore be good places to look for one in Florida.

size.length: About five inches long, with a wingspan around eight inches.

species.habitat: Breeds in mature boreal spruce-fir forest, typically stands 25 to 75 years old with trees exceeding 35 feet. During migration it uses a wide variety of wooded and shrubby habitats — conifers are preferred but deciduous trees, thickets, and even palm trees are used. In Florida and the Caribbean it turns up in parks, gardens, coffee plantations, scrub, and mangrove edges.
species.where_to_look: Scan the upper parts of trees during migration, especially branch tips where birds search for insects. Also check flowering trees and shrubs: Cape May Warblers sometimes come lower to drink nectar. The weeping bottlebrush in the park is the kind of nectar-rich flowering tree worth checking.
species.when_to_see: Primarily a migrant through Florida, especially during spring and fall, with some birds wintering in southern Florida. Palma Sola has recorded the species in spring, but there are too few park observations to establish a local seasonal pattern.

seasonality.note: Passage migrant through Florida and occasional winter visitor. Palma Sola records are currently too limited to define a local peak.

interaction.guidance: Watch from the path and avoid following a feeding bird from tree to tree. If one is visiting flowers, staying back may let it return repeatedly to the same plant.

conservation.status: Globally classified as Least Concern, but long-term monitoring has documented substantial population declines. Its numbers also fluctuate with outbreaks of spruce budworm on the breeding grounds.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Palm Warblers characteristically bob the tail. Cape May Warblers have a short tail, streaked breast and slightly downcurved bill.
Yellow-rumped Warblers show a brighter yellow rump. A dull Cape May shows finer streaking below and a slimmer, slightly downcurved bill.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: Cape May Warblers usually forage high in trees, picking insects from foliage and branch tips and sometimes flying out to catch insects in the air. Migration occurs mostly at night.
Outside the breeding season they also visit flowers for nectar and may defend productive flowering plants from other nectar feeders.

species.teaser: It was named for Cape May, New Jersey, after an early specimen was collected there — even though Cape May is neither its breeding nor its main wintering home.

quick_hits: One of the most ground-loving warblers in North America — it walks rather than hops, and bobs its tail almost without stopping. It is also one of only three Setophaga warblers (alongside Prairie and Kirtland's) that pump their tails incessantly. Researchers think the habit may serve as a pursuit-deterrent signal, telling watching predators: 'I see you, I'm quick, don't bother.'

Despite the name, it rarely perches in palms. The name traces to 1789, when German naturalist Johann Friedrich Gmelin described the species from a wintering specimen collected on the palm-rich Caribbean island of Hispaniola — not from any real affinity for the trees.

Two subtly different forms visit Florida each winter: the brighter 'Yellow' Palm Warbler along the Gulf Coast and the drabber 'Western' form along the Atlantic side, with both mixing across the peninsula.
It heads north earlier than almost any other warbler, sometimes beating other species back to the boreal forest by nearly two months.
species.range_and_origin: The Palm Warbler breeds in open sphagnum bogs and coniferous forest edges across Canada and the northeastern United States, with roughly 98 percent of the global population nesting in Canada's boreal forest. In winter it moves to the southeastern United States, the Caribbean, and Central America as far south as Panama. Florida is one of its most important wintering grounds, with birds present in open and scrubby habitats across the state from October through April.
more_information: The Palm Warbler is the most terrestrial member of its genus — and one of only three Setophaga warblers (alongside Prairie and Kirtland's) that pump their tails incessantly. It spends far more time on the ground than any other wood-warbler, walking with an upright, pipit-like posture.
This constant tail-bob is visible at any distance and in any plumage, making it one of the easiest warblers to identify by behavior alone.

Why the tail-bob? Ornithologists think it may function as a pursuit-deterrent signal, essentially advertising to lurking predators that the bird has spotted them and is fit enough to escape. Research on phoebes and other tail-pumping birds supports this idea, though the exact function in Palm Warblers has not been tested directly. For now the bob remains one of nature's cheerful small mysteries.

Two subspecies reach Florida each winter — and they essentially swap directions to get here. The 'Yellow' Palm Warbler (S. p. hypochrysea) breeds in the eastern boreal forest and migrates southwest to winter mainly along the Gulf Coast, making it the form most likely seen at Palma Sola. The drabber 'Western' form (S. p.
palmarum) breeds farther west and migrates southeast to winter along the Atlantic side; both overlap broadly across the Florida peninsula, giving visitors a chance to compare them side by side.

On the wintering grounds, Palm Warblers form loose foraging flocks and join mixed groups with sparrows, Yellow-rumped Warblers, and Ruby-crowned Kinglets. They primarily eat insects gleaned from the ground and low shrubs, supplemented by berries and seeds such as bayberry and sea grape when available.

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: A small, somewhat stocky brownish-olive warbler with bright yellow undertail coverts visible in every plumage and season. Upright, pipit-like posture on the ground; tail bobs nearly without pause.

blocks.label: Breeding plumage
blocks.text: Rusty chestnut cap, yellow eyebrow stripe, dark eyeline, and rufous streaking on the breast. Eastern 'Yellow' birds are more extensively yellow below; western birds show a whitish belly with yellow restricted to the undertail and throat.

blocks.label: Winter plumage
blocks.text: Cap turns dull brown, overall impression is washed-out and pale. The yellow undertail coverts and pale eyebrow remain the most reliable marks. Rufous breast streaking is still present but fainter.

identification.what_to_look_for: Bright yellow undertail coverts flashing with each tail-bob are the single most reliable field mark year-round. Also look for a pale eyebrow stripe, a dark line through the eye, and a subtle rusty wash to the breast streaks. The upright, ground-walking posture distinguishes it instantly from most other warblers.

species.diet: Primarily insects — beetles, flies, caterpillars, aphids, and spiders — picked from the ground or low shrubs, with occasional aerial sallies for flying prey. In winter, also eats berries and seeds including bayberry, sea grape, and hawthorn.
species.behavior: Walks on the ground more than any other wood-warbler, bobbing its tail almost incessantly whether foraging, perching, or moving between shrubs. Forms loose winter flocks, often associating with sparrows and Yellow-rumped Warblers. Occasionally sallies into the air for insects like a small flycatcher.
species.sounds: Song is a weak, buzzy, monotonous trill — described as similar to a Chipping Sparrow but slower and less crisp. Call is a sharp 'chek' or 'tsip,' often given in flight.
species.ecological_role: A significant insect predator on its wintering grounds, helping suppress populations of beetles, flies, caterpillars, and other invertebrates. Also disperses seeds of berries consumed in winter. As one of the most abundant winter warblers in Florida, it is a meaningful link in park and garden food webs.

size.lifespan: not well documented on average; the oldest banding record stands at 6 years and 7 months

species.habitat: Winters in open, scrubby, and edge habitats: weedy fields, forest edges, coastal scrub, marshes, mangroves, parks, and gardens. Avoids dense closed-canopy forest. Breeds in sphagnum bogs with scattered spruce, tamarack, and cedar in the boreal forest far to the north.
species.where_to_look: Check open grassy or weedy areas, low shrubs, and ground-level leaf litter throughout the park. Palm Warblers spend far more time on the ground than other warblers, so scan low rather than up into the canopy. They often associate with sparrows and Yellow-rumped Warblers in loose winter flocks. The tail-bob is visible from a distance.
species.when_to_see: A reliable winter visitor, typically present from October through early April. Most active during daylight hours. Peak numbers occur mid-November through February. Spring departure begins in late February and early March; the species moves north earlier than almost any other warbler.

seasonality.note: Common winter visitor.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

species.internal_notes: Added 2026-06-19 from iNat observations export (June 2026 batch). Content drafted; at research status pending iNat photo collection + licensing, then promotion to html.

how_it_lives.text: It walks on the ground more than any other warbler, and the tail bobs almost without stopping — foraging, perched, moving between shrubs, it keeps going. That bob is the identification.

Mostly insects picked off the ground and low shrubs: beetles, flies, caterpillars, aphids, spiders. It will also sally into the air after something flying, like a small flycatcher. In winter it adds berries and seeds — bayberry, sea grape, hawthorn.
Winter flocks are loose and mixed, often with sparrows and yellow-rumped warblers.

quick_hits: A plain, grayish-brown bird that sits upright on an exposed perch, wags its tail, and darts out to catch a flying insect — that is an eastern phoebe.
The tail-wagging is almost constant and is the quickest way to recognize it — few other small birds pump their tail so persistently.
It calls its own name: a burry, two-note 'fee-bee' that it repeats from a favorite perch.
A winter visitor to Florida, it breeds farther north and returns each fall.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. Breeds across the eastern U.S. and southern Canada; winters in the southeastern U.S. and Mexico. A winter visitor in the Bradenton area.
more_information: The eastern phoebe is a flycatcher — a bird that hunts by sallying out from a perch to snatch insects in midair, then returning to the same perch. It is one of the most reliable 'sit-and-wait' hunters in the bird world.
The persistent tail-wagging is diagnostic. It pumps its tail almost continuously, whether perched or just after landing — a habit that immediately narrows the ID.
It was the first bird ever banded in North America — John James Audubon tied silver thread to a phoebe's leg in 1804 to see if it would return the next year. It did.

blocks.label: Shape
blocks.text: Upright posture, medium-sized flycatcher. Plain grayish-brown above, pale below.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Wags persistently — the best field mark.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Small and dark — a flycatcher bill.

blocks.label: Voice
blocks.text: A burry 'fee-bee' repeated from a perch.

identification.what_to_look_for: A plain gray-brown bird on an exposed perch, wagging its tail and darting out after insects.

species.diet: Flying insects — caught by sallying from a perch. Some berries in winter.
species.behavior: Sits on exposed perches, pumps tail, darts out to catch insects. Returns to the same perch. Solitary.
species.sounds: A burry, emphatic 'fee-bee' — says its name.
species.ecological_role: Flying-insect predator; the first bird banded in North America (Audubon, 1804).
species.plant_connections: Perches on exposed branches; eats some berries in winter.

size.lifespan: commonly several years.

species.habitat: Open areas with perches — forest edges, fences, buildings, park structures.
species.where_to_look: Exposed perches near open ground — fences, low branches, building edges. Watch for the tail-wag.
species.when_to_see: Winter visitor — typically October through March.

seasonality.note: Breeds to the north; winters in Florida.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: It picks an exposed perch, pumps its tail, darts out to take an insect in the air, and comes back to the same spot. Then does it again.
Flying insects almost entirely, with some berries in winter. Usually alone.

quick_hits: The American robin — brick-red breast, dark back, yellow bill — is one of the most recognized birds in North America, but in Florida it is a winter visitor, not a year-round neighbor.
It arrives in large flocks in fall, feeding on berries and worms across lawns and open ground, then heads north to breed.
Despite its name, it is not closely related to the European robin — early colonists just thought the red breast looked familiar.
A robin on a Florida lawn in January is on vacation; by April it is usually back up north nesting.
species.range_and_origin: Native to North America. Breeds across the U.S. and Canada; winters in the southern U.S. including Florida. A seasonal visitor here.
more_information: The American robin is arguably the most familiar bird in North America — but in Florida it is a seasonal guest, arriving in flocks from late fall and departing by spring.
In winter it shifts from its summer diet of earthworms and insects to one dominated by berries and fruit, and large flocks can strip a fruiting tree in hours.
Its presence on a Florida lawn is a good seasonal marker: if you see robins, it is probably winter.

blocks.label: Breast
blocks.text: Warm brick-red to orange.

blocks.label: Back
blocks.text: Dark gray-brown.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Yellow.

blocks.label: Behavior
blocks.text: Runs across lawns, pauses, tilts head, then pulls up a worm.

identification.what_to_look_for: A plump, upright bird with a red breast hopping across a lawn. In Florida, a winter visitor in flocks.

species.diet: Earthworms and insects (summer); berries and fruit (winter).
species.behavior: Runs across open ground, tilts head to listen for worms. Forms large flocks in winter. Feeds heavily on fruit.
species.sounds: A rich, caroling song ('cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio') — but mostly heard on the breeding grounds, not in Florida.
species.ecological_role: Berry disperser in winter; earthworm and insect predator in summer.
species.plant_connections: Heavy berry consumer in winter — disperses many native and ornamental fruit species.

size.lifespan: commonly a few years.

species.habitat: Lawns, parks, open ground, and berry-producing trees and shrubs.
species.where_to_look: Open lawns and under fruiting trees in winter.
species.when_to_see: Winter visitor — typically November through March.

seasonality.note: Breeds far to the north; present in Florida only in the cold months.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

how_it_lives.text: On a lawn it runs a few steps, stops, and cocks its head — not listening, as it looks, but getting one eye on the ground to catch a worm moving.
Earthworms and insects through the warm months. In winter the diet swings almost entirely to fruit, and robins that fed alone all summer turn up in flocks.

quick_hits: A small, fast butterfly checkered in gray, white, and dark charcoal — darting low over open ground and landing flat to bask in the sun.
Males develop a dusting of blue-gray hairs on the body and wing bases that gives them a frosty, cool-toned look.

It is a spread-winged skipper (subfamily Pyrginae) — the 'fighter jet' family of butterflies. While grass skippers hold their wings angled up like a tent at rest, spread-winged skippers bask with wings laid completely flat.
Common in sunny, weedy, open areas — exactly the kind of wild edges a botanical park preserves.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern U.S., Caribbean, and tropical Americas. Year-round resident in southern Florida.
more_information: The tropical checkered-skipper is one of the more recognizable skippers thanks to its bold checkered wing pattern of gray, white, and dark marks. Males get an additional dusting of blue-gray hairs that gives them a distinctive frosty appearance.

It belongs to the spread-winged skippers (subfamily Pyrginae). When basking, these butterflies lay their wings completely flat — a quick field clue that instantly separates them from grass skippers, which angle their wings upward like a tent.

It is a butterfly of disturbed, open ground — roadsides, gardens, weedy lots, and park edges — where its caterpillar host plants grow. Look for fanpetals and wireweed (Sida species) in sunny weedy patches; what looks like a nuisance weed is a nursery for this skipper.

blocks.label: Pattern
blocks.text: Bold checkered gray, white, and dark pattern on the wings.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Frosty blue-gray hair on the body and wing bases.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Fast, low, darting — typical skipper.

blocks.label: Posture
blocks.text: Basks with wings spread completely flat — the signature of a spread-winged skipper (Pyrginae), not a grass skipper.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small, fast, checkered gray-and-white butterfly basking flat on the ground or low vegetation in an open, sunny, weedy area.

species.diet: Caterpillars feed on plants in the mallow family (Malvaceae) — especially fanpetals and wireweed (Sida rhombifolia and Sida acuta), which grow as common 'weeds' in open ground. Adults sip nectar from small flowers, particularly Sida species, Frogfruit (Phyla nodiflora), and Spanish Needles (Bidens alba).
species.behavior: Fast, darting flight close to the ground. Basks with wings open. Males patrol low over open ground.
species.ecological_role: Pollinator of low flowers including Frogfruit and Spanish Needles; caterpillars feed on mallow-family plants (Sida species and relatives), making roadside 'weeds' an essential part of its life cycle.
species.plant_connections: Caterpillar host plants are mallows (Malvaceae). Adults nectar at many low flowers.

size.lifespan: adult lifespan not specifically documented for this species; typical of short-lived skippers

species.habitat: Disturbed open ground, gardens, roadsides, weedy lots.
species.where_to_look: Open, sunny, weedy areas and garden edges. Watch for the fast, low flight.
species.when_to_see: Year-round in southern Florida, most numerous in warm months.

danger.people: Harmless.

Caterpillars feed on the mallow family, especially fanpetals and wireweed — plants most people would call weeds. Adults nectar at small flowers, particularly those same sidas, frogfruit and Spanish needles.

quick_hits: A dragonfly with orange-and-brown banded wings — like a tiny Halloween decoration perched on a plant stem near the pond.
It perches at the very tip of a stem and flutters in the breeze like a flag, which is unusual for a dragonfly — most prefer rigid, still perches.
Males patrol territories over open water, but they spend long stretches resting on stem tips between patrols.
The wing pattern makes it one of the easiest dragonflies to identify at a glance.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the eastern United States. Common in Florida near ponds and wetlands.
more_information: The Halloween pennant is one of the most recognizable dragonflies in the eastern U.S. thanks to its bold orange-and-brown wing bands — a pattern that immediately suggests its common name.
Unlike most dragonflies that prefer rigid perches, it often lands on the tips of flexible stems and sways in the breeze, fluttering like a small pennant or flag.
Like all dragonflies, it is a precision aerial predator, catching small insects in flight.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Orange-amber with dark brown bands — the Halloween pattern.

blocks.label: Perch
blocks.text: Sits at the very tip of flexible stems, swaying in the breeze.

blocks.label: Body
blocks.text: Yellowish to orange body.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Medium dragonfly, wingspan about 3 inches.

identification.what_to_look_for: A dragonfly with boldly banded orange-and-brown wings perched at the tip of a stem near water.

species.diet: Small flying insects, caught in the air.
species.behavior: Perches on flexible stem tips and flutters in the wind. Males patrol open water. Aerial hunter.
species.ecological_role: Aerial insect predator; part of the pond-edge food web.
species.plant_connections: Perches on emergent wetland vegetation.

size.lifespan: adults live a few weeks.

species.habitat: Ponds, marshes, and wetland edges.
species.where_to_look: Stem tips near the ponds. Look for the distinctive wing pattern and swaying perch.
species.when_to_see: A warm-season dragonfly, most common spring through fall.

how_it_lives.text: It perches on the flexible tip of a stem and lets the wind move it, wings held out. That is the easiest way to find one: look for the stalk that is swaying differently from everything around it.
Males patrol open water. The hunting happens in the air — small flying insects, taken on the wing.

quick_hits: The enormous, brightly colored grasshopper lumbering across the path — too big and too slow to be any other species — is an eastern lubber.

It can barely fly. Those tiny wings are essentially useless for flight, so it walks, climbs, and hops instead. The name 'lubber' comes from an old word meaning clumsy or slow — fitting for an insect that has traded speed for attitude.

The bold yellow, orange, and black adult pattern and the jet-black nymphal stripe are aposematic warning coloration, an honest advertisement to birds and reptiles that this insect is toxic and tastes terrible.

Most predators learn quickly to leave it alone. The loggerhead shrike, however, skewers the grasshopper on a thorn or barbed wire and waits up to several days for the toxins to break down before eating it.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States. Common in Florida year-round.
more_information: The eastern lubber is the unmistakable giant of Florida's grasshoppers — up to three inches long, painted in warning colors, and moving with a slow, confident waddle that says 'I dare you.' The name 'lubber' traces to an old English word for a clumsy, heavy person, which suits this insect perfectly.

That confidence is earned. When harassed, it hisses, spreads its tiny wings to flash bright colors, and forces air and fluid through its thoracic spiracles to generate a foul-smelling chemical foam containing plant-derived compounds including phenols, quinones, and terpenes. These are sequestered from the plants it eats and repel virtually every predator that tries it.

The bold adult coloration and the juvenile's black-with-red-stripe pattern are both examples of aposematic warning coloration — a visual signal that tells birds and reptiles the insect is unpalatable before they even attempt an attack.

The loggerhead shrike (Lanius ludovicianus) has found a workaround. It skewers the lubber on a thorn or barbed wire and leaves it exposed for up to several days, allowing the defensive chemicals to degrade, then eats the safe remains — sometimes discarding the chemical-laden thorax entirely.

Juveniles are jet-black with a distinctive yellow, orange, or red stripe and red-marked legs — looking so different from the adults that visitors frequently mistake them for a separate species. They emerge in spring, grow through five (occasionally six) nymphal instars, and reach full adult coloration in about 40 to 60 days.

Females deposit subterranean egg pods containing 30 to 50 eggs at a depth of roughly 1¼ to 2 inches in the soil, where they overwinter for six to eight months before hatching in spring. The lubber's one-generation-per-year cycle is tightly synchronized with Florida's seasonal plant growth.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Up to 3 inches — by far the largest grasshopper you will see.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Adults are yellow to orange with bold black markings. Juveniles are strikingly different: glossy jet-black with a vivid yellow, orange, or red stripe running the length of the body and red-tinged legs. They look so unlike the adults that visitors routinely mistake them for a different species — they are not.

blocks.label: Wings
blocks.text: Tiny, vestigial — cannot support flight.

blocks.label: Behavior
blocks.text: Slow, deliberate walker. Does not jump far or fly.

identification.what_to_look_for: In spring, watch for small glossy black nymphs with a bright red, orange, or yellow stripe — unmistakably lubbers in their juvenile form. By summer, those same insects grow into large, boldly patterned yellow-and-black adults lumbering slowly along paths or through garden beds. Both stages are big, bold, and easy to spot.

species.diet: Broadly polyphagous — recorded feeding on plants from more than 38 families. In Florida gardens, plants in the family Amaryllidaceae (especially Amaryllis and Crinum lilies) are particularly favored, along with Agapanthus, Narcissus, oleander, and citrus. Can cause significant defoliation of ornamental beds.
species.behavior: Walks slowly and deliberately. When threatened, hisses, spreads tiny wings, and produces toxic foam.
species.sounds: A hissing sound when threatened.
species.ecological_role: Herbivore with a wide host-plant range and a mild garden-pest reputation. Its potent chemical defenses make it toxic to most vertebrate predators, functioning as a chemical dead-end in the food web. The loggerhead shrike is its primary known avian predator, defeating the toxins by aging impaled carcasses before consumption.
species.plant_connections: Feeds on many garden and wild plants.

size.lifespan: about one year (one generation per year).

species.habitat: Gardens, roadsides, fields, and open woodland — common in disturbed habitats.
species.where_to_look: Paths, garden beds, and low vegetation. Hard to miss when present.
species.when_to_see: Most visible spring through fall; juveniles emerge in spring.

seasonality.note: Juveniles appear in spring; adults most visible summer through fall.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: It walks. Slowly, deliberately, and without much interest in getting away from you. Threaten it and it hisses, spreads its useless little wings, and produces a toxic foam.

how_it_lives.label: What it eats in a garden
how_it_lives.text: Almost anything — recorded on plants from more than thirty-eight families. In Florida gardens it goes hardest at the amaryllis family, especially amaryllis and crinum lilies, along with agapanthus, narcissus, oleander and citrus. A few of them can strip an ornamental bed.

quick_hits: A small, dark rabbit with short ears and a tiny brownish tail — not the long-eared cottontail most people picture when they hear 'rabbit.'
It is one of the very few rabbits that swims, and it does so willingly — wading into water to escape predators or to reach better feeding areas.
Unlike cottontails, the marsh rabbit's tail is not white and fluffy — it is small, brown, and inconspicuous.
It is a true Florida native, tied to the state's wetlands, marshes, and dense, damp vegetation.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States from Virginia to Florida. Year-round resident in Florida's wetlands.
more_information: The marsh rabbit is the rabbit of Florida's damp places — swamps, pond edges, marshes, and dense wet thickets. It is smaller and darker than the eastern cottontail, with proportionally shorter ears and a dingy brown tail instead of the cottontail's white powder puff.

Its willingness to swim sets it apart from most rabbits. When threatened, it may plunge into water and swim with only its nose above the surface, or sit motionless in shallow water among emergent vegetation.
It is most active at dawn and dusk, feeding on grasses, sedges, and aquatic plants.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Small — smaller than a cottontail, about 14 to 16 inches.

blocks.label: Ears
blocks.text: Short for a rabbit.

blocks.label: Tail
blocks.text: Small, brown — not the white 'cotton ball' of a cottontail.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Dark brown to blackish-brown, darker than a cottontail.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small, dark rabbit near water with short ears and no white tail. If it runs toward water instead of away, it is a marsh rabbit.

species.diet: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, and other low vegetation — a strict herbivore.
species.behavior: Crepuscular — most active at dawn and dusk. Swims readily. Freezes when threatened before bolting.
species.ecological_role: Herbivore and prey animal — a food source for hawks, owls, bobcats, and snakes.
species.plant_connections: Feeds on grasses, sedges, and wetland plants.

size.lifespan: commonly 1 to 4 years in the wild.

species.habitat: Marshes, wet thickets, pond edges, and dense vegetation near water.
species.where_to_look: Along pond edges and in dense low vegetation, especially at dawn or dusk.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident, most visible at dawn and dusk.

seasonality.note: Crepuscular; rarely seen in midday.

danger.people: Harmless.

how_it_lives.text: Most active at dawn and dusk, feeding on grasses, sedges and whatever low green growth is at hand. Strictly a plant eater.
Two things separate it from a cottontail. It swims — readily, and well. And when something alarms it, it freezes before it runs, which is often the only reason you get a look at one.

quick_hits: The only breeding hummingbird in the eastern United States — a tiny, jewel-green bird that hovers at flowers and feeders, beating its wings about 53 times per second.
The male's throat blazes iridescent ruby-red in the right light — turn your head and it looks black. The color is structural, not pigmented, created by microscopic platelets in the feathers.
Every fall, many cross the Gulf of Mexico nonstop — roughly 500 miles of open water with nowhere to land.
It weighs about as much as a penny, yet it is fiercely territorial and will chase birds many times its size away from a flower patch.
species.range_and_origin: Native to eastern North America. Breeds across the eastern U.S. and southern Canada; winters in Central America. Present in Florida mainly during migration and winter, though some breed in the northern part of the state.
more_information: The ruby-throated hummingbird is the default hummingbird of the eastern United States — the only species that regularly breeds east of the Mississippi. Its tiny size, hovering flight, and iridescent plumage make it one of the most charismatic visitors to any garden.

To fuel its metabolism, it visits hundreds of flowers per day and also eats tiny insects and spiders for protein. Its heart beats over 1,200 times per minute in flight, and it enters a torpor-like state overnight to conserve energy.
In the Bradenton area it is most likely during fall and spring migration, with some wintering birds.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Tiny — about 3 inches long, weighing roughly a tenth of an ounce.

blocks.label: Male
blocks.text: Iridescent green above, white below, with a brilliant ruby-red throat (gorget) that can look black.

blocks.label: Female

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Hovers in place, wings beating so fast they blur.

identification.what_to_look_for: A tiny hovering bird at flowers or feeders. Males flash a ruby-red throat in the right light. Listen for the humming of the wings.

species.diet: Nectar from flowers and feeders; tiny insects and spiders for protein.
species.behavior: Hovers to feed. Fiercely territorial — chases other hummingbirds and larger birds from flower patches. Incredibly fast and agile.
species.sounds: A rapid, chittering series of notes; the hum of the wings is often the first clue.
species.ecological_role: Pollinator of tubular flowers; insect predator. A key player in the pollination of many native wildflowers.
species.plant_connections: Visits many native and garden flowers, especially tubular red, orange, and pink blooms.

size.lifespan: commonly 3 to 5 years, occasionally much longer.

species.habitat: Gardens, woodland edges, and flowery areas during migration.
species.where_to_look: Around the flower beds, especially tubular blooms. Listen for the wing hum.
species.when_to_see: Most likely during fall and spring migration; some winter here. A seasonal visitor.

seasonality.note: Arrives in March as spring migration moves north; passes through again August through October heading south. A small number may linger into winter in sheltered coastal spots, but reliable presence for Manatee County is March through October.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: It feeds hovering, wings beating too fast to see, and it does not share. A hummingbird will chase off other hummingbirds and birds several times its size to keep a patch of flowers to itself.
Nectar from flowers and feeders for fuel, and tiny insects and spiders for protein — sugar alone will not build a bird.

quick_hits: The brown pelican is the one that dives — plunging headfirst from the air into the water to scoop up fish, unlike the white pelican which scoops from the surface.
It is a conservation comeback: nearly eliminated by DDT in the 1960s and 70s, it recovered after the pesticide was banned and was removed from the endangered list in 2009.
The massive bill and expandable throat pouch can hold roughly three gallons of water — which it drains before swallowing the fish.
Despite the big bill, an adult weighs only about eight pounds — surprisingly light for a bird that looks so heavy.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the Americas. Year-round resident along the Florida coast.
more_information: The brown pelican is the only pelican in the world that hunts by plunge-diving. It spots fish from the air, folds its wings, and drops headfirst into the water — hitting at enough speed to stun small fish, which it scoops up in its enormous throat pouch.

Its recovery from DDT is one of the landmark conservation stories. The pesticide thinned eggshells to the point of collapse, and pelican populations crashed. After DDT was banned in 1972, populations slowly recovered, and the species was delisted in 2009.
Gulls and other birds often try to steal fish right from the pelican's pouch as it drains the water — an occupational hazard.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Large, heavy-bodied, with a massive bill and throat pouch.

blocks.label: Color
blocks.text: Gray-brown body, dark belly, white to yellowish head. Breeding adults show a dark chestnut nape.

blocks.label: Flight
blocks.text: Flies low over water in lines, alternating flaps and glides.

blocks.label: Feeding
blocks.text: Plunge-dives headfirst — the only pelican that does this.

identification.what_to_look_for: A large brown-and-gray pelican flying low over water or plunge-diving. Distinguished from the white pelican by color and the diving behavior.

species.diet: Fish — caught by plunge-diving from the air.
species.behavior: Plunge-dives for fish. Flies in formation low over the water. Rests on pilings and docks.
species.ecological_role: Fish predator in coastal and nearshore waters; an indicator of marine ecosystem health.

size.lifespan: commonly over 25 years.

species.habitat: Coastal waters, bays, estuaries, and nearshore areas.
species.where_to_look: Overhead or on nearby water — a flyover visitor to the park, not a pond bird. More likely near the coast.
species.when_to_see: Year-round along the coast; occasional flyovers at the park.

seasonality.note: Coastal bird; park sightings are flyovers.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe and enjoy.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: Watch one fish and you will see the dive: it climbs, folds, and hits the water hard enough to hear from the bank. Fish, caught that way and no other.
The rest of the time it is loafing on a piling or a dock rail, or flying low along the water in a line with others, wingtips almost touching the surface.

quick_hits: A compact white egret standing in a field next to cattle or mowing equipment — not at the water's edge — is almost certainly a cattle egret.
It is the only egret in Florida that forages primarily on dry land, following large animals and machinery to catch the insects they stir up.
It arrived in the Americas on its own, crossing the Atlantic from Africa in the 1940s and spreading rapidly across the continent — a natural colonizer, not an introduction.
In breeding plumage it flushes with patches of orange-buff on the head, chest, and back.
species.range_and_origin: Originally from Africa. Naturally colonized South America in the 1870s and North America by the 1940s–50s. Now a common year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The cattle egret is a remarkable natural success story. Without any human assistance, it crossed the Atlantic from Africa and colonized the New World, reaching Florida by the 1950s and spreading across the continent within decades.

Its trick is its feeding strategy: instead of hunting in water like other egrets, it follows large animals — cattle, horses, tractors — and snaps up the grasshoppers, crickets, and other insects they disturb. This terrestrial niche was largely unoccupied, which is part of why it spread so fast.
Despite being a recent arrival, it is not considered invasive — it filled an open niche without displacing native species.

blocks.label: Habitat
blocks.text: Dry fields and lawns, not water — the key distinction from other egrets.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Compact and stocky — smaller and thicker-necked than a snowy egret.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Short, stout, yellow to orange.

blocks.label: Breeding
blocks.text: Patches of orange-buff on head, chest, and back.

identification.what_to_look_for: A compact white egret in a field or lawn, often near livestock or mowing equipment. Stockier and shorter-necked than other egrets, with a yellow bill.

species.diet: Insects — grasshoppers, crickets, flies, and other invertebrates flushed by large animals or machinery.
species.behavior: Follows livestock and mowers on foot. Gregarious — often in loose groups. Nests colonially.
species.sounds: Generally quiet; croaks at the colony.
species.ecological_role: Insect predator in agricultural and open-ground habitats. A natural colonizer that filled an unoccupied niche.
species.plant_connections: Nests colonially in trees near water, though it forages far from it.

size.lifespan: commonly several years.

species.habitat: Fields, lawns, pastures, and open ground — near livestock or mowers.
species.where_to_look: Open grassy areas, especially if mowing is happening nearby. Not at the water's edge.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident.

danger.people: Harmless.

how_it_lives.text: It hunts by following something bigger. Cattle, a tractor, a mower — anything that walks through grass and flushes insects out ahead of it. The egret walks behind and picks off what jumps.
Grasshoppers, crickets, flies. Usually in loose groups, and it nests in colonies.

quick_hits: A medium white egret with a black bill, black legs, and bright yellow feet — as if it is wearing golden slippers.
The bright yellow feet are a feeding tool: it shuffles them through the water to stir up small fish and shrimp, then strikes.
A century ago it was nearly wiped out for its lacy breeding plumes, just like the great egret — and its recovery helped fuel the early Audubon movement.
Smaller and more active than the great egret, it dashes and darts through the shallows rather than standing still.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the Americas. Year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The snowy egret is the energetic counterpart to the patient great egret. Where the great egret stands motionless and waits, the snowy runs, hops, and shuffles its feet to flush prey — a distinctly different hunting style.

The golden-yellow feet are the single best field mark. In breeding plumage, it also grows delicate, recurved plumes on its back, head, and chest — the same plumes that made it a target for the millinery trade in the late 1800s.
Its recovery is one of the early triumphs of the conservation movement, though more recently its numbers in some areas have declined again with wetland loss.

blocks.label: Feet
blocks.text: Bright yellow — the 'golden slippers.' The single best field mark.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Black and slender.

blocks.label: Legs
blocks.text: Black.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.text: Medium — about 24 inches, smaller than the great egret.

identification.what_to_look_for: A medium white egret actively running through shallows. Check the feet: if they are yellow, it is a snowy egret.

species.diet: Small fish, shrimp, crabs, insects, and aquatic invertebrates — often flushed with foot-shuffling.
species.behavior: Active, energetic hunter — runs, shuffles feet, and strikes rapidly. More animated than other egrets.
species.sounds: Generally quiet; some harsh squawks at the colony.
species.ecological_role: Predator of small aquatic animals; historically a flagship for the conservation movement.
species.plant_connections: Forages in wetland vegetation; nests colonially in trees near water.

size.lifespan: commonly up to 17 years.

species.habitat: Wetlands, ponds, marshes, tidal flats — any shallow water.
species.where_to_look: Pond edges and shallows, often actively running and shuffling. Look for the yellow feet.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident.

danger.people: Harmless.

conservation.status: Least Concern. Common and widespread.

how_it_lives.text: The busiest of the egrets. Where a great egret stands still and waits, this one runs, stops, stirs the bottom with a bright yellow foot to flush something out, and stabs at whatever moves.
Small fish, shrimp, crabs, insects. The foot-shuffling is the giveaway — no other white heron here feeds like that.

quick_hits: A small, dark-blue heron stalking the shallows — quiet, solitary, and easy to overlook next to the showier egrets.
Young birds are entirely white, and often mistaken for snowy egrets — the blue comes in gradually during their first year, creating a patchy, piebald look.
The white-to-blue transition may be a survival strategy: white juveniles are tolerated by snowy egret flocks, gaining safety in numbers until they can fend for themselves.
It is a State Threatened species in Florida — its numbers have declined with wetland loss.
species.range_and_origin: Native to the southeastern United States, Caribbean, and Central and South America. Year-round resident in Florida.
more_information: The little blue heron is one of the quieter wading birds — it lacks the dramatic plumes of the great egret and the pink flash of the spoonbill, but it is a skilled, patient hunter of small fish, frogs, and crustaceans.

The juvenile plumage trick is remarkable: young little blue herons are entirely white, looking almost exactly like snowy egrets. Scientists believe this lets them join snowy egret flocks, where more eyes mean more safety from predators. As they mature, blue feathers gradually replace white, creating a mottled, calico look before they settle into full adult blue.
It is listed as State Threatened in Florida, part of a broader decline in wading bird populations linked to wetland loss and degraded water quality.

blocks.label: Adult
blocks.text: Entirely dark slate-blue with a purplish head and neck. Dark-tipped bill.

blocks.label: Juvenile
blocks.text: Entirely white — easily confused with a snowy egret.

blocks.label: Molting immature
blocks.text: Patchy blue-and-white, a unique calico look.

blocks.label: Bill
blocks.text: Gray with a dark tip — not the yellow bill of an egret.

identification.what_to_look_for: A small, dark-blue heron hunting alone in the shallows. If you see a white heron with a gray-tipped bill instead of yellow, it may be a juvenile little blue.

species.diet: Small fish, frogs, crayfish, and aquatic insects — stalks slowly in shallow water.
species.behavior: Patient, slow stalker. Hunts alone more often than in flocks. Quiet and unobtrusive.
species.ecological_role: Wading bird predator of small aquatic animals; an indicator of wetland health.
species.plant_connections: Forages in wetland vegetation; nests in trees near water.

size.lifespan: commonly 7 years or more.

species.habitat: Freshwater and saltwater wetlands, pond edges, marshes.
species.where_to_look: Pond edges and shallows, often alone. Look for the dark blue adult or the white juvenile with a gray-tipped bill.
species.when_to_see: Year-round resident.

danger.people: Harmless.

interaction.guidance: Observe from a distance. As a State Threatened species, avoid disturbing it.

conservation.status: State Threatened in Florida. Numbers have declined due to wetland loss and water-quality degradation.
